19	physiological potential of athletes"; Technical, "To acquire cognitive technical skills and
20	attain the desired level of technical mastery"; Tactical, "To acquire cognitive sport-specific
21	tactics, which allow for the most effective utilization of athlete's motor and technical
22	abilities in competition"; Psychological, "To develop the athlete's personality so that it is
23	harmonious, highly motivated and morally stable. To instill the skills of cognitive
24	self-regulation of the athlete's emotional state in order to facilitate maximum realization of
25	their psycho-physiological potential"; Intellectual, "To improve athletes' general and
26	sport-specific knowledge in order to effectively complete their training and competitive
27	program." No book title or page number is given beyond the year.

30	categories; it does not explain why training is best divided into exactly these five domains
31	rather than some other number, nor does it cite empirical support for the division.

33	lecturer uses later, for example the "Training Process" slide in U4 L1 p.4 which lists the
34	same five domains and then explicitly narrows the coach's own scope ("Tactical: Limited to
35	zero influence. Technical: Limited to zero influence") to argue why a strength coach's

18	"Uncovering the system's forming factors" - factors "can stem from general knowledge about
19	the theory and methods of training, scientific findings, experiences of the nation's best
20	coaches, and the approaches used by other countries"; (2) "Determining the system's
21	structure" - "a model for both short- and long-term training should be created," applicable
22	by all coaches but "flexible enough that coaches can enrich the system's structure based upon
23	their own experiences"; (3) "Validating the efficacy or effects of the system" - evaluated
24	"in a multidimensional manner," from simple performance-improvement outcomes to "direct
25	measurements of physiological adaptation, such as hormonal or cell signaling adaptations," to
26	"mechanical assessments... maximal anaerobic power, maximal aerobic power, maximal force
27	generating capacity, and peak rate of force development," with sport scientists named as

15	
16	**What it is** - Evans's slides (U1 L4 p.17-22) present two distinct regulatory models. He
17	credits "1935 - Walter Cannon" with Homeostasis: "Processes in the organism to preserve
18	constant conditions within which are centered around specific set points and governed by
19	negative feedback loops" (p.15). He credits "Sterling & Sayer in 1988" (the slide's spelling;
20	the well-known 1988 paper is by Sterling and Eyer) and "Jay Schulkin" with Allostasis: "Process
21	by which an organism achieves internal viability through a bodily change of state," further
22	distinguishing "Allostatic State" ("Chronic OVER-ACTIVATION of regulatory systems and the
23	alterations of body set points") from "Allostatic Overload" ("expression of pathophysiology
24	by the chronic over-activation of regulating systems") (p.17). A direct-comparison slide
25	(p.19) credited to "Bruce McEwen" states: "Homeostasis describes mechanisms that HOLD
26	CONSTANT a controlled variable by sensing its deviation from a 'setpoint' and feeding back to
27	correct the error. Allostasis describes mechanisms that CHANGE a controlled variable by
28	predicting what level will be needed and overriding local feedback to meet anticipated
29	demand." The worked example given is blood pressure: "120/80 is 'normal.' What happens if it
30	jumps up to 150/100?" with the answer, credited to "(Sterling, Eyer, 1998)" on the following
31	slide (note: this citation year, 1998, differs from the 1988 year given two slides earlier for
32	the same Sterling and Eyer source; the slide deck does not reconcile this discrepancy, so both
33	years are recorded here as they appear): "Brain sets blood pressure via multiple, mutually
34	reinforcing mechanisms. Negative feedback mechanisms are acutely overridden. When demand
35	persists, all mechanisms are reset to operate at the new level."
36	
37	**Why it works** - The slides state the distinction (fixed setpoint with feedback correction,
38	versus a setpoint that shifts to anticipate demand) but do not explain the underlying neural
39	or endocrine mechanism connecting a training stimulus to a shifted setpoint beyond the blood

41	mechanisms" without detailing what those mechanisms are. Inference: applied to training
42	adaptation, the distinction implies that some training-induced changes (e.g., a durably raised
43	resting heart rate range under chronic overreaching) may be better modeled as an allostatic
44	setpoint shift than as homeostatic disturbance-and-recovery, but Evans does not make this
45	application explicit in this lecture; it is a plausible follow-on question left open by his

47	(U1 L4 p.26-33), which are not atomized as a separate entry in this ingest because they

20	Overreaching, Functional (FOR) (timescale: days/weeks; outcome: temporary decrease, then
21	recovery); Overreaching, Nonfunctional (NFOR) (timescale: weeks/months; outcome: decrease or
22	no change, recovery takes weeks to months); Overtraining (timescale: months to a year+;
23	outcome: decrease, recovery takes months to a year or more). Functional Overreaching is
24	further defined (p.12): "Stimulates physiological adaptations, which compensate for
25	training-related stress. Recovery can take days to weeks depending on the stimulus
26	magnitude." Nonfunctional Overreaching (p.13): "Occurs when intensified training is continued
27	and results in the stagnation or decreases in performance that would require longer recovery
28	times. When NFOR is continued for a long period of time, the athlete will eventually reach a
29	state of overtraining." Overtraining (p.14): "a process of excessive training & non-training
30	stressors in high performance athletes that may lead to persistent fatigue, performance
31	decrements, neuroendocrine changes, alterations in mood states, and frequent illness," most

14	# Evans's Own Conclusion: No Definitive Diagnostic Tool for Overtraining Syndrome Exists
15	
16	**What it is** - After surveying eight "hypothetical mechanisms" of overtraining syndrome
17	(OTS) across biochemistry, cardiovascular/HRV, immune system, hormonal, brain, training
18	status, psychometrics, and psychomotor speed (U3 L2 p.2-16), Evans's closing slide (p.17),
19	titled "Reality and OTS," states in his own words: "Definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not
20	available. The human organisms of made up of many biological systems that are independent
21	and dependent upon each other, and the interaction between them is contextual on the
22	readiness and preparedness of those systems, the imposed stimuli, and the adaptation path the
23	individual makes to cope with the stressor. The reliance of adopting sound training theory
24	principles, and performance monitoring will continue to be paramount to keep athletes
25	improving in their respective sport." Along the way, he makes several specific negative
26	claims: on hormonal markers, "Testosterone / Cortisol ratio used to be considered the
27	overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (p.12); on immune markers, "there is NO evidence
28	to low glutamine levels with impaired immune function" (p.11); on the literature generally,
29	"Research seems to be relatively scarce since ensuring OTS is difficult... The biggest issue
30	with the literature is the TIME at which they are studying high level athletes" (p.10).
31	
32	**Why it works** - This is Evans's own synthesized conclusion after reviewing multiple
33	candidate biomarker systems, not a mechanism claim; he does not assert that any single system
34	(hormonal, immune, HRV) is more reliable than the others, but rather that none is sufficient
35	alone, and that multi-system interaction is itself part of why no single diagnostic exists.
36	Inference: the practical implication is that overtraining should be inferred from the
37	convergence of multiple imperfect signals (training status, performance trend, and whichever
38	biomarkers a program can afford) rather than from any one test result in isolation.
39	
40	**When to apply** - As a caution against over-relying on any single monitoring metric (HRV,
41	cortisol, testosterone/cortisol ratio, glutamine) as a stand-alone overtraining diagnostic.
42	This is directly consistent with Eric's baseline's own documented shift away from a single
43	metric: the department replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI
44	specifically because the surveys "couldn't be trusted" as a sole signal, and mRSI itself is
45	one part of a broader monitoring approach, not the sole diagnostic
46	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
47	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Eric's baseline's tension #3 (coach's-eye-first versus
48	objective-first) is also relevant context: Evans's conclusion here does not resolve that
49	tension, since it recommends "sound training theory principles, and performance monitoring"
50	together, without specifying how to weigh a coach's qualitative judgment against quantitative
51	monitoring when they disagree.
52	
53	**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans's specific negative claims (testosterone/cortisol
54	ratio no longer the "gold standard"; no evidence linking low glutamine to impaired immune
55	function) are stated without a named citation in this lecture; treat them as his professional

# Evans's Own Conclusion: No Definitive Diagnostic Tool for Overtraining Syndrome Exists

**What it is** - After surveying eight "hypothetical mechanisms" of overtraining syndrome
(OTS) across biochemistry, cardiovascular/HRV, immune system, hormonal, brain, training
status, psychometrics, and psychomotor speed (U3 L2 p.2-16), Evans's closing slide (p.17),
titled "Reality and OTS," states in his own words: "Definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not
available. The human organisms of made up of many biological systems that are independent
and dependent upon each other, and the interaction between them is contextual on the
readiness and preparedness of those systems, the imposed stimuli, and the adaptation path the
individual makes to cope with the stressor. The reliance of adopting sound training theory
principles, and performance monitoring will continue to be paramount to keep athletes
improving in their respective sport." Along the way, he makes several specific negative
claims: on hormonal markers, "Testosterone / Cortisol ratio used to be considered the
overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (p.12); on immune markers, "there is NO evidence
to low glutamine levels with impaired immune function" (p.11); on the literature generally,
"Research seems to be relatively scarce since ensuring OTS is difficult... The biggest issue
with the literature is the TIME at which they are studying high level athletes" (p.10).

**Why it works** - This is Evans's own synthesized conclusion after reviewing multiple
candidate biomarker systems, not a mechanism claim; he does not assert that any single system
(hormonal, immune, HRV) is more reliable than the others, but rather that none is sufficient
alone, and that multi-system interaction is itself part of why no single diagnostic exists.
Inference: the practical implication is that overtraining should be inferred from the
convergence of multiple imperfect signals (training status, performance trend, and whichever
biomarkers a program can afford) rather than from any one test result in isolation.

**When to apply** - As a caution against over-relying on any single monitoring metric (HRV,
cortisol, testosterone/cortisol ratio, glutamine) as a stand-alone overtraining diagnostic.
This is directly consistent with Eric's baseline's own documented shift away from a single
metric: the department replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI
specifically because the surveys "couldn't be trusted" as a sole signal, and mRSI itself is
one part of a broader monitoring approach, not the sole diagnostic
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Eric's baseline's tension #3 (coach's-eye-first versus
objective-first) is also relevant context: Evans's conclusion here does not resolve that
tension, since it recommends "sound training theory principles, and performance monitoring"
together, without specifying how to weigh a coach's qualitative judgment against quantitative
monitoring when they disagree.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans's specific negative claims (testosterone/cortisol
ratio no longer the "gold standard"; no evidence linking low glutamine to impaired immune
function) are stated without a named citation in this lecture; treat them as his professional
summary of a literature he does not cite by author or year here, not as independently
verified facts. Do not use this entry to argue that monitoring is worthless; Evans's own
conclusion explicitly retains "performance monitoring" as "paramount," only rejecting the idea
of a single definitive diagnostic test. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific athlete case is given; this is a literature-survey conclusion.

**Related** - [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]] (U4 L1, Evans's later monitoring-process framework,
consistent with treating no-single-metric-is-sufficient as a design constraint).

19	you do what you do. Example: Max strength may be important in the preparation, but in the
20	wrong place, it can have negative interactions." A following slide (p.19) restates this as:
21	"The interaction & interdependence of the training components. No training component is in
22	isolation. Timing NOT time." And (p.20): "To have the team or individual ready to perform at

competition phase and one major peak," recommended "FOR NOVICE AND JUNIOR ATHLETES. LONG
PREPARATORY PHASE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TECHNICAL/TACTICAL/PHYSICAL DOMAINS," with a
stated week distribution per 52-week cycle: Preparatory >= 32 weeks, Competitive 10-15 weeks,
Transition 5 weeks. Bicycle: "TWO competition phases and two major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR
ELITE ATHLETES WHO QUALIFY FOR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS. TRY TO KEEP THE PREPARATORY PHASES AS
LONG AS POSSIBLE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT," distribution per 26-week cycle: Preparatory 13 weeks,
Competitive 5-10 weeks, Transition 3 weeks. Tricycle: "THREE competition phases and three
major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR INTERNATIONAL-LEVEL ATHLETES. SOLID FOUNDATION IS INSTALLED AND
THEY CAN TOLERATE MULTIPLE PEAKS. 3 OR MORE," distribution per 17-18-week cycle: Preparatory
>= 8 weeks, Competitive 3-5 weeks, Transition 2-3 weeks. No book title beyond "Bompa" and the
year 2009 is given on the slides.

**Why it works** - The slides state the recommended athlete level and week distribution for
each cycle type but do not explain the physiological reasoning for why, for example, a
tricycle's shorter preparatory phase (>=8 weeks versus a monocycle's >=32) is appropriate only
for athletes who already have "a solid foundation... installed" - the mechanism (a trained
athlete needing less time to re-establish base qualities before specializing toward a peak) is
implied by the athlete-level guideline but not stated explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** - As a first-pass structural choice when designing an annual plan: how many
distinct peaks does the competition calendar actually require, and does the athlete's training
age support the correspondingly shorter preparatory phases of a multi-cycle plan? Eric's
baseline's own annual-plan language treats the plan as "a flexible roadmap, not a fixed
contract," built around "the competition calendar, key non-training dates... and phase-by
-phase volume/intensity waves" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23`) without naming a specific monocycle/bicycle/
tricycle choice; this framework gives that flexible planning language a specific named
structural menu to choose from. For a sport like college football, with a single primary
competitive season, this framework's monocycle category (long preparatory phase, one major
peak window covering the season) is the closest fit among the three named here, though Evans
does not apply this specific framework to football in this lecture (his football example in

cycle types it uses).

15	
16	**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.26-30), cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011," present a
17	"Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities" framework with two named components relevant
18	to this entry. Integration: "the way motor capacity is trained in the annual plan; in
19	relation to the others," with two options: "Complex" ("Biomotor Abilities Are All Trained At
20	The Same Time") or "Sequential" ("Biomotor Abilities Are Emphasized At Different Times During
21	The Annual Plan"). Development: "the way each conditional motor capacity is trained during
22	the annual plan," with three named patterns: Complex development, illustrated at three
23	timescales - within a training unit ("MxS, Power, Muscular Endurance are trained within this
24	sequence within a single training session"), within a microcycle ("MxS, Power, ME are all
25	trained in the microcycle in different training workouts"), and within a mesocycle ("MxS,
26	Power, ME are trained throughout the mesocycle, during dedicated microcycles"); Sequential
27	development, distinguishing "Immediate Realization" ("At the end of the mesocycle, the
28	indexes of the trained biomotor quality are improved") from "Delayed Realization" ("At the
29	end of the mesocycle, the indexes... are depressed but improve later"); and Pendular
30	development ("Two qualities of biomotor abilities are trained in alternative fashion (e.g.,
31	Max Strength followed by Power followed by Max Strength followed by Power)"). No book title is
32	given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."
33	
34	**Why it works** - The slides name the integration and development options and give brief
35	illustrative examples (MxS/Power/ME sequencing; the delayed-realization pattern) but do not
36	state the physiological mechanism for why a given quality shows delayed rather than immediate
37	realization, or how to predict in advance which pattern a given combination of qualities will
38	follow; this is presented as a descriptive taxonomy of observed or theorized patterns, not a
39	derived model.
40	
41	**When to apply** - As vocabulary for describing how a program is choosing to combine
42	multiple biomotor qualities: are strength, power, and endurance work happening together
43	(complex) or in separate blocks (sequential), and within complex training, at what
44	timescale (session, microcycle, or mesocycle) is that combination happening? This connects
45	directly to Eric's baseline's training-compatibility constraint - incompatible qualities are
46	not trained together at full intensity, compatible ones are trained together, and the rest at
47	a retention dose (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
48	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`) - which is effectively a rule for choosing
49	between this framework's Complex and Sequential integration options based on quality
50	compatibility, though the baseline material does not use Buzzichelli's specific vocabulary.

itself in the sport-specific movement pattern; he does not, in this slide, specify which of the
five Dynamic Correspondence criteria weight-room exercises typically fail, only that "minimal
DC criteria" are met in general.

**When to apply** - As a caution against treating weight-room testing (1RM lifts, jump tests
performed in isolation from the sport skill) as a direct proxy for on-field performance,
without denying that weight-room training itself contributes to Special Work Capacity. This
connects directly to a broader theme in Eric's baseline: "A test can be scientifically valid
and still be the wrong choice operationally... even a valid test stops being valuable" without
the infrastructure and interpretation context to use it well (`method-baseline.md`,
"Philosophy and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`).
Evans's claim here is a related but distinct point: not about operational sustainability of a
test, but about a testing method's inherent limits in predicting a different outcome (field
performance) than the one it directly measures (weight-room capacity).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans does not name which specific weight-room exercises
he has in mind, nor does he give an example of measuring "how well" a given weight-room result
predicted (or failed to predict) actual field performance for any real athlete; this is a
conceptual claim, not a data-backed one, in this lecture. He also does not specify a threshold
for "minimal DC criteria met" versus a higher, more sport-corresponding threshold that would
change this conclusion. Confidence is untested. Do not read this claim as recommending against
weight-room training generally; Evans explicitly disclaims that reading in the same breath he
makes the claim.

**Example** - No specific exercise-to-sport-skill comparison is worked through in this
lecture; the wrestling takedown analysis from U2 L4 (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]]) is the course's only
detailed worked Dynamic Correspondence example, applied to a competitive skill rather than to
a weight-room exercise directly.

**Related** - [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]],
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]].

# National Sport-Science "Systems" Are Implied to Track with Olympic Success

**What it is** - U1 L2 p.2 places four national/organizational sport-science systems side by
side with a one-line political or institutional tag each: "Soviet Union, 1950s, Communism";
"German Democratic Republic, 1950s, Socialism"; "Australian Sports Commission" (no date or
tag given, illustrated with a photo that Inference (reviewer knowledge, not on the slide)
identifies as an Australian Institute of Sport image, so the slide names the AIS only by
picture, not by text); and "UK Sport" with a table of UK medal rankings across five Olympics:
1996, 36th; 2000, 10th; 2004, 10th; 2008, 4th; 2012, 3rd. The following page (p.4) shows a chart
of men's 100m Olympic sprint times from 1972-2012, annotated "US Boycott" at the 1980 dip and
"Usain Bolt" at the 2008-2012 drop below 9.7s. Evans does not connect these two slides with
any explicit sentence; they appear back to back with no linking text.

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism connecting UK Sport's establishment (Inference
(reviewer knowledge, not on the slide): UK Sport was created in 1997) to the medal-rank
improvement shown. Inference: the juxtaposition is meant to suggest that centralized,
government-funded sport-science investment (the pattern shared by the Soviet Union, GDR, and
UK Sport examples) correlates with improved medal outcomes, but the slide presents no
comparison group, no control for other factors (population, funding levels, doping history in

(Sport Scientist), Anatoliy Bondarchuk (Coach), Henk Kraaijenhof (Coach), Atko Viru and Mehis
Viru (Sport Scientist / Coach, starred, sharing one line), Charlie Francis (Coach, starred),

(Sport Scientist / Coach), Al Vermeil (Coach), Johnny Parker (Coach), and Dan Pfaff (Coach).

low-resolution video still, disconnected from the named-giants list, with no other text.

argued history. Inference: the list moves roughly from foundational Soviet motor-control and
periodization theory (Bernstein, Matveyev) through Soviet/Eastern-bloc training-methods

who studied or translated that material (Kraaijenhof, Francis, Yessis, Bompa, Issurin,

# Increasing Power Output Is the Final Goal of Training for Competition Exercise

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.6) quotes Yuri Verkhoshansky, 2011, directly: "May
almost always be related to the capacity to express power produced by the speed of movements
and by the force of overcoming external resistance," and "Consequently, the training process,
focused on improving the sports result, represents the process of increasing the POWER
OUTPUT of competition exercise." The following slides define power mathematically (Work per
unit time, Watts; Power = Force x Velocity, p.7) and give two "factors in increasing power
output": a biomechanical perspective ("Human movement is an interaction between the human
body and the external environment (Bernstein)," p.8) and a physiological perspective ("Human
movement represents an interaction between the human organism and the external environment
(Verkhoshanksy)," p.9, sic on the spelling). The book does not give the original publication
this 2011 quote is drawn from.

**Why it works** - The quoted passage states power output as the training objective but does
not itself explain the physiological mechanism by which force x velocity training raises
competitive power output; the slide's "biomechanical" and "physiological perspective" bullets
restate the interaction-with-environment framing rather than supplying a causal chain.
Inference: linking this claim to the later "Two Factors to Increase Sport Result" slide (p.14,
see [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]]) suggests Evans's
intended chain is: competitive result depends on power output, power output depends on
force x velocity capacity specific to the sport (special work capacity) plus the skill to
apply it (technical mastery) - but this chain is Inference, built by the entry writer across
two slides, not stated as a single argument by Evans himself.

**When to apply** - As a framing question when evaluating any strength or power program:
does this exercise or method plausibly raise the force x velocity output specific to the
competitive movement, or is it improving something else (e.g., general work capacity,
hypertrophy) that may or may not transfer? Eric's baseline: it does not use this exact
Verkhoshansky quote, but its programming philosophy independently emphasizes exercise
selection along a general-to-competitive spectrum and matching training to the "amplitude/
direction of movement... dynamics of effort... rate/timing of force production" (`method
-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence,
Verkhoshansky). Inference: this is consistent with (though not identical to) this
power-output framing.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives no numeric example of measuring "power
output of competition exercise" for any actual sport skill, and no citation locator (book
title, page) for the 2011 Verkhoshansky quote beyond the year. Do not treat "power output" as
a single measurable variable without specifying which movement and which units; the
comparison later in the same lecture between a "sprinter" and a "marathoner" (p.13) implies
the relevant power-output value is sport-specific, but the slide gives no numbers for either.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The lecture's only example is qualitative: a "SPRINTER vs. MARATHONER" power
output comparison slide (p.13) with no numbers, framed as "these changes are dependent on...
the demands of the sport."

**Related** - [[framework--anokhin-functional-system-three-subsystems]],
[[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]].
</content>

# Anokhin's Functional System: Central Nervous, Neuromuscular, and Energy-Supplying Subsystems Gathered Into One

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.10) credits "P. Anokhin" with a model in which the
"Human Organism" and "Its physiological systems" (Central nervous system, Neuromuscular
system, Energy-supplying system) are "Activated & Gathered into" a "FUNCTIONAL SYSTEM." The
next slide (p.12) states each subsystem's specific job in this functional system: the Central
nervous system's role is "Increasing capacity to produce the necessary intensity of impulses
from the central motor area to the periphery and to ensure appropriate intra and
inter-muscular coordination"; the Neuromuscular system's role is "Improving the function of
the motor apparatus in accordance with the work regime"; the Energy-supplying system's role
is "Enhancement of the energy providing sources and setting up the marriage between them."
The slide gives no citation year or source text for Anokhin's model.

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism for how these three subsystems are
"activated and gathered" into a single functional system beyond naming Anokhin as the
originator; it presents the three-part division and each part's stated role as given facts,
not as something derived from data shown on the slide. Inference: this framing appears
designed to argue that improving "power output" (the topic of the surrounding slides, see
[[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]]) requires improving all
three subsystems together, not any one in isolation, since the model calls them a single

# Special Work Capacity and Technical Mastery Are "The Two Factors to Increase Sport Result"

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.14) states "THE TWO FACTORS to INCREASE SPORT
RESULT" as "Special Work Capacity and Technical Mastery," defined in a two-column table:
Special Work Capacity is "Motor potential (power generators) that are specific to the sport";
Technical Mastery is "Skills to coordinate maximal force efforts OR to rationally employ
force efforts." No author or citation is given for this specific two-factor framing on this
slide (contrast with the surrounding slides, which name Verkhoshansky and Anokhin
explicitly). This exact framing recurs twice more in the course: verbatim as the opening
slide of the Unit 4 summary lecture (U4 L3 p.2), and as the U4 L1 p.5 slide headed "Most
Important: Special Work Capacity... Movement & Energetic potential relative to the sporting
demands."

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism for why only these two factors (and not, for
example, psychological or tactical factors, which Evans's own later monitoring lecture lists
as separate training domains at U4 L1 p.4 and p.8, see
[[framework--issurin-five-training-domains]]) determine sport result; it is presented as a
given division, not derived. Inference: because the definition of Special Work Capacity
explicitly says "specific to the sport," and Technical Mastery is defined as the skill to
deploy force efforts, this pairing functions as Evans's own compressed restatement of the
"power output requires both the capacity and the skill to express it" idea introduced two
slides earlier (see [[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]]),
rather than a new, independently sourced claim.

**When to apply** - As a two-part diagnostic when an athlete's competitive performance is
below expectation: is the limiter their sport-specific motor/energetic capacity, or their
skill in applying the capacity they already have? Evans returns to exactly this framing in
U4 L1 p.5 to argue that weight-room exercises "provide little insight on how they will
perform on their respective field of play" because they meet "minimal Dynamic Correspondence
criteria" with the sport skill - see [[claim--weight-room-transfer-limited-without-dynamic
-correspondence]] for that specific, stronger claim. Eric's baseline: it does not use this
exact two-factor label, but its emphasis on matching exercise selection to the competitive
skill via Dynamic Correspondence (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") addresses the
same underlying question of capacity versus applied skill.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a two-way division asserted without citation or
elaboration; the slide does not explain how to measure either factor independently, or how to
tell which one is limiting a given athlete. Do not treat this as an exhaustive account of
what determines sport result; Evans's own later psychological, tactical, and intellectual
"Training Process" domains (U4 L1 p.4, echoing Issurin's five domains, see
[[framework--issurin-five-training-domains]]) sit outside this two-factor model, which the
slide does not reconcile against it. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - Not given on this slide; the closest worked example in the course is the
10-step annual-plan build for a football wide receiver (U3 L7). Inference: this implicitly
targets both factors (bioenergetic/biodynamic/biomotor sequencing for Special Work Capacity,
exercise classification for Technical Mastery) without naming this two-factor model
explicitly. See [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]].

**Related** - [[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]],
[[claim--weight-room-transfer-limited-without-dynamic-correspondence]],
[[framework--issurin-five-training-domains]].
</content>

# Special Work Capacity and Technical Mastery Are "The Two Factors to Increase Sport Result"

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.14) states "THE TWO FACTORS to INCREASE SPORT
RESULT" as "Special Work Capacity and Technical Mastery," defined in a two-column table:
Special Work Capacity is "Motor potential (power generators) that are specific to the sport";
Technical Mastery is "Skills to coordinate maximal force efforts OR to rationally employ
force efforts." No author or citation is given for this specific two-factor framing on this
slide (contrast with the surrounding slides, which name Verkhoshansky and Anokhin
explicitly). This exact framing recurs twice more in the course: verbatim as the opening
slide of the Unit 4 summary lecture (U4 L3 p.2), and as the first bullet under "Training
Process" in U4 L1 p.5 ("Most Important: Special Work Capacity... Movement & Energetic
potential relative to the sporting demands").

**Why it works** - The slide gives no mechanism for why only these two factors (and not, for
example, psychological or tactical factors, which Evans's own later monitoring lecture lists
as separate training domains, see [[framework--adime-monitoring-process]]) determine sport
result; it is presented as a given division, not derived. Inference: because the definition
of Special Work Capacity explicitly says "specific to the sport," and Technical Mastery is
defined as the skill to deploy force efforts, this pairing functions as Evans's own
compressed restatement of the "power output requires both the capacity and the skill to
express it" idea introduced two slides earlier (see
[[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]]), rather than a new,
independently sourced claim.

**When to apply** - As a two-part diagnostic when an athlete's competitive performance is
below expectation: is the limiter their sport-specific motor/energetic capacity, or their
skill in applying the capacity they already have? Evans returns to exactly this framing in

criteria" with the sport skill - see [[claim--weight-room-transfer-limited-without-dynamic
-correspondence]] for that specific, stronger claim. Eric's baseline does not use this exact

# Issurin's Five Domains of the Training Process: Physical, Technical, Tactical, Psychological, Intellectual

**What it is** - Evans's slide "The Training Process" (U1 L3 p.15, repeated verbatim as
"Training Domains" at U2 L4 p.4), cited to "(Issurin, 2008)," gives a five-row table of
Domain and Purpose: Physical, "To improve physical (motor) abilities and increase the
physiological potential of athletes"; Technical, "To acquire cognitive technical skills and
attain the desired level of technical mastery"; Tactical, "To acquire cognitive sport-specific
tactics, which allow for the most effective utilization of athlete's motor and technical
abilities in competition"; Psychological, "To develop the athlete's personality so that it is
harmonious, highly motivated and morally stable. To instill the skills of cognitive
self-regulation of the athlete's emotional state in order to facilitate maximum realization of
their psycho-physiological potential"; Intellectual, "To improve athletes' general and
sport-specific knowledge in order to effectively complete their training and competitive
program." No book title or page number is given beyond the year.

**Why it works** - The slide states the five domains and each one's stated purpose as given
categories; it does not explain why training is best divided into exactly these five domains
rather than some other number, nor does it cite empirical support for the division.
Inference: U4 L1 p.4 uses the table to bound the strength coach's influence (Physical,
Psychological, Intellectual active; Tactical and Technical "Limited to zero influence"). The
monitoring slides then list the five domains (p.8) and narrow to "Purely Physiological" (p.9),
which suggests monitoring is scoped to the physical domain.

**When to apply** - As a checklist when scoping what "training" a role is actually
responsible for; Evans's own later use of this table (U4 L1 p.4) is to argue that a strength
and conditioning coach has real influence over three of the five domains and should not
overreach into Tactical or Technical. Eric's baseline: its four departmental operating
principles (Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance,
Performance Team Collaboration, Research and Development) are a different taxonomy for a
different purpose (departmental scope, not training-domain scope) and do not map one-to-one
onto Issurin's five domains (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles").
Inference: both are attempts to bound a role's responsibility.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a secondary citation (Evans citing Issurin) with
no book title, edition, or page given; the entry writer has not independently verified this
table against Issurin's original text (Issurin's "Block Periodization" book is separately
staged in this library at `block-periodization--issurin`, but its ingest map does not show
this exact five-domain table among its atomized Chapters 1-3 entries as of this ingest).
Treat the wording above as Evans's slide transcription, not a verified quotation of Issurin.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - Evans's own applied example is in U4 L1 p.4: he assigns himself (as strength
coach) an active role in Physical ("Build bigger, more efficient engines"), Psychological
("Pocket psychologist, surrogate parent, cheerleader"), and Intellectual ("Mentor and
educator of the training process... Influence them to be their own manager") domains, while
explicitly disclaiming Tactical and Technical influence.

**Related** - [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: if
`block-periodization--issurin` later atomizes a matching five-domain table from Issurin's own
text (Chapters 4-5 remain pending as of this ingest), link back here to confirm or correct
this secondary citation.
</content>

# Morphobiomechanics: A Seven-Type Constitutional Body Classification

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U2 L3 p.20) credits "Dorohov, RN and Guba, VP from Smolensk
State Academy of Physical Education, Sport and Tourism, Division of Anatomy and Biomechanics"
with a "morphobiomechanics" system naming seven constitutional body types: Mesosomatic (MeS),
Microsomatic (MiS), Macrosomatic (MaS), Megalosomatic (MegS), Nanosomatic (NanS),
Micromesosomatic (MiMeS), and Mesomacrosomatic (MeMaS). The slide states the system is
"Designed to differentiate different human body constitutional types (anthropometry, muscle
mass structure, bone structure, body fat mass)" but gives no definition of what distinguishes
any one of the seven types from another, no cutoff values, and no citation year or source
publication.

**Why it works** - The slide names the concept without elaboration, per the source's own
sparse-slide format; it gives no criteria for classifying an athlete into one of the seven
types, so no mechanism can be extracted beyond the stated purpose (differentiating body
constitution across anthropometry, muscle mass, bone structure, and body fat).

**When to apply** - Not currently applicable in practice from this lecture alone; the slide
does not provide enough information to classify an athlete or interpret what training
implications follow from a given type. It is recorded here as a named framework Evans
introduced, should the CVASPS transcript or another source later supply working definitions
of each of the seven types. Eric's baseline: it does not reference this classification system
or any equivalent constitutional-type framework; its anthropometric material focuses on
Performance Nutrition-owned body composition tracking, capped at four times per year
(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition"). Inference: this is a different
measurement purpose (composition tracking over time, not constitutional-type classification).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This entry cannot be used to classify a real athlete: no
definitions, thresholds, or worked examples are given anywhere in this lecture for any of the
seven type names. Do not infer body types from name etymology alone (e.g., assuming
"Macrosomatic" means simply "large body") without a primary source, since the slide gives no
such definitions. Confidence is untested, and this is one of the clearest cases in this
course of "the slide names a concept without elaboration," per the task brief's rule for this
source.

**Example** - Not given anywhere in this lecture.

**Related** - `supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model.md`
(the nearest constitutional-type idea staged in this library - "Structure (somatotype, size,
shape)" - a different model from morphobiomechanics's seven named types, not a duplicate). No
other existing entry in the vault or staging library matches "morphobiomechanics" or any of
the seven type names (checked by grep across both).
</content>

# Bondarchuk's Three Principles of Training-System Construction

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U2 L4 p.7-10), headed "System of Training" and credited to
"(Bondarchuk)" with no year or title given, present three sequential principles: (1)
"Uncovering the system's forming factors" - factors "can stem from general knowledge about
the theory and methods of training, scientific findings, experiences of the nation's best
coaches, and the approaches used by other countries"; (2) "Determining the system's
structure" - "a model for both short- and long-term training should be created," applicable
by all coaches but "flexible enough that coaches can enrich the system's structure based upon
their own experiences"; (3) "Validating the efficacy or effects of the system" - evaluated
"in a multidimensional manner," from simple performance-improvement outcomes to "direct
measurements of physiological adaptation, such as hormonal or cell signaling adaptations," to
"mechanical assessments... maximal anaerobic power, maximal aerobic power, maximal force
generating capacity, and peak rate of force development," with sport scientists named as
playing "a very important role" in this validation step, and the system subject to
re-evaluation and modification "if the training system is not optimal."

**Why it works** - This is a process model (how to build and validate a training system), not
a claim about a specific physiological mechanism, so no "why it works" mechanism applies; the
slide's own logic is that a system should be built from evidence and coaching experience
(step 1), formalized but adaptable (step 2), and then continuously checked against outcomes
data across multiple measurement levels (step 3), closing the loop back to step 2 if it is not
working.

**When to apply** - As a three-step audit for any training system a program is running or
considering adopting: has it been built from a stated evidence base (step 1), does it have a
documented, transferable structure (step 2), and is it being evaluated against measured
outcomes with a defined path to revision (step 3)? Eric's baseline: the Playbook Development
Plan names missing pieces at exactly steps 2 and 3 of this model - no documented
sport-specific data dictionaries or daily operational checklists (step 2's "model... that can
be applied by all coaches"), and no standardized coach-facing reporting templates yet built
(step 3's evaluation loop) (`method-baseline.md`, "Department model and roles," "Data,
technology and reporting," citing `performance-playbook-development-plan.md`). Inference:
this maps closely onto Eric's own department gap analysis; Eric's baseline's own stated
three-phase roadmap (Foundation, Operational Depth, Education and Culture, ending in an
annual Playbook review cycle) is a structurally similar build-then-validate-then-revise
pattern, independently arrived at for a different specific purpose (departmental
documentation, not a single training system).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives no book title or year for "(Bondarchuk)",
so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this ingest; the
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk` book already staged in this library does not (as

system-construction model, so it is recorded here as a distinct, not-yet-cross-checked claim,
not confirmed against Bondarchuk's own text. Confidence is untested. Do not treat "sport
scientists can play a very important role" as evidence that this validation step is
routinely followed in practice; the slide states it as a recommendation, not an observed
norm.

# Evans's Worked Example: Applying the Five Dynamic-Correspondence Criteria to a Wrestling Clinch Takedown

**What it is** - After presenting the standard five Dynamic Correspondence criteria
(amplitude/direction of movement, accentuated region of force production, dynamics of effort,
rate and time of maximum force production, regime of muscular work - the same five-factor
list Eric's baseline independently records as course material; Eric's baseline:
`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence,
Verkhoshansky), Evans's slides (U2 L4 p.21-22) work through a specific technique: "Takedown
from a clinch that is executed from the position of having low double under hooks secured
against the lower back of the opponent." His analysis, quoted directly: amplitude/direction -
"Lifting the opponent begins in an upward rotational fashion that allows the hips to
transition for the downward rotational movement during the throw towards the mat... The
amplitude of hip and back extension is rather small as the lift is initiated from a

# Three Types of Overload: Stimulating, Retaining, Detraining

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U2 L4 p.15) names "3 Types of Overload": (1) Stimulating -
"Magnitude of the training load is above the neutral level - heightened adaptation"; (2)
Retaining - "Magnitude is in the neutral zone - maintained preparedness"; (3) Detraining -
"Magnitude of the training load leads to a decrease in performance, the functional
capabilities of the athlete, or both." No author or citation is given for this specific
three-way naming on this slide, though it appears in the same lecture segment as other
Bondarchuk- and Issurin-cited material.

**Why it works** - The slide defines each overload type by its outcome (heightened
adaptation, maintained preparedness, or decreased performance) relative to an unnamed
"neutral level," but does not state how to measure or identify that neutral level for a given
athlete; no mechanism is given for why loads above versus at versus below that level produce
these three different outcomes, beyond the general adaptation-stimulus logic given on the
preceding slide (U2 L4 p.14: "Increasing stimulus -> adaptation -> performance improvement...
Lack of stimulus -> plateau... Excessive stimulus -> maladaptation -> decrease in
performance").

**When to apply** - As a three-way classification for describing the intent of a given
training block or phase: is this phase meant to stimulate new adaptation, retain current
fitness during a competing priority (e.g., in-season), or is it a planned detraining/deload
period. Eric's baseline: its in-season rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). Inference: this functions as a
Retaining-type overload strategy in this framework's terms, though the baseline material does
not use this specific three-way vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives no numeric or percentage definition of the
"neutral level" that separates Stimulating from Retaining from Detraining loads for any
specific biomotor quality or athlete population; without that, this framework is a labeling
scheme for outcomes observed after the fact, not a prospective dosing tool. No citation is
given, so its origin (Bondarchuk, Issurin, or Evans's own synthesis of the surrounding cited
material) cannot be confirmed from this slide alone. Inference: a deliberate deload would only
fit "Detraining" if it lowers performance; the slide defines the type by that outcome, not by
whether the reduction was planned. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No worked example with specific loads or athletes is given in this lecture.

**Related** - The "3 Basic Scenarios" slide (U2 L4 p.14) and the continuum slide (U2 L4 p.16,
a four-way "Undertraining / Overreaching / Overtraining" version plus Acute overload) share
this stimulus-to-outcome logic; see also
[[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (U3 L1) for Evans's later, more detailed
overtraining-specific version of this same underlying dose-response logic. Inference
(unverified reviewer suggestion, not yet checked against a primary source): the
stimulating/retaining/detraining terms with a "neutral zone" resemble Zatsiorsky and Kraemer,
*Science and Practice of Strength Training* (a listed HHPR 5355 textbook, `method-baseline.md`
line 219); if confirmed by a future reviewer, name it as the likely origin.
</content>

# "Intensity Will Define the Biological Target. Volume Is How Deep You Want to Go."

**What it is** - Evans's closing slide on Training Load (U2 L6 p.20), titled "Intensity &
Volume...", presents both lines in quotation marks with no attribution: "Intensity will
define the biological target." "Volume is how deep you want to go." This follows earlier
slides in the same lecture defining Intensity as "a function of neuromuscular activation
(NA)," with NA pattern "dictated by the external load, the speed of performance, the amount
of fatigue accrued, and the type of exercise undertaken" and noting a psychological dimension
("Something can have LOW strain yet high psychological strain," p.15), and Volume as "time or
duration of training... the distance covered or the volume load in RT (volume = reps x sets x
resistance)... Volume for different biomotor qualities need to be compared amongst
themselves. You cannot compare mobility volume to maximal strength volume" (p.13).

**Why it works** - The slide does not explain the physiological mechanism connecting a given
intensity level to a specific "biological target" (e.g., which intensity range targets which
energy system or fiber type is not stated on this slide, though it is addressed elsewhere in
the course, e.g. the energy-system power/capacity tables in U2 L1); this is offered as a
compact planning heuristic, not a mechanism claim. Inference: read alongside the volume
definition's caveat that different biomotor qualities' volumes are not directly comparable,
the heuristic's practical implication is that a coach should first fix the intensity (which
determines what quality is being trained) before deciding how much volume (how much of that
specific quality) to prescribe, rather than planning volume and intensity independently.

**When to apply** - As a quick planning check when writing a training block: has the
intensity been set first, to establish which biological quality is actually being targeted,
before volume is added within that target? Eric's baseline: it does not use this specific
phrase, but its Prilepin's-chart-based approach to daily rep/set assignment by percentage of
1RM (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19`) operates on a structurally similar premise: pick
the intensity zone (percentage of 1RM) first, then assign volume (reps and sets) within it.
Evans's own U2 L6 p.17 shows a Jovanovic/Prilepin effort-level chart in this same lecture, so
this is a point of convergence with the baseline's Prilepin-chart practice, not only an
analogy.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a compact aphorism, not a quantified model; the
slide itself gives no specific intensity thresholds or their associated "biological targets."
U2 L6 p.16-18 in the same lecture supply the intensity-to-target tables (six intensity zones
by % of maximum performance at p.16, the Jovanovic/Prilepin effort-level chart at p.17,
Borilkievich (1982) five training zones with HR and lactate bands at p.18), so it should not
be applied mechanically without that more detailed content. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific numeric example is given on this slide.

**Related** - None found elsewhere in this library under this specific phrasing.
</content>

# Homeostasis Holds a Setpoint Constant; Allostasis Changes the Setpoint to Meet Anticipated Demand

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U1 L4 p.17-22) present two distinct regulatory models. He
credits "1935 - Walter Cannon" with Homeostasis: "Processes in the organism to preserve
constant conditions within which are centered around specific set points and governed by
negative feedback loops" (p.15). He credits "Sterling & Sayer in 1988" (the slide's spelling;
the well-known 1988 paper is by Sterling and Eyer; Inference (reviewer knowledge): this is the
entry writer's outside identification, not stated on the slide) and "Jay Schulkin" with
Allostasis: "Process by which an organism achieves internal viability through a bodily change
of state," further distinguishing "Allostatic State" ("Chronic OVER-ACTIVATION of regulatory
systems and the alterations of body set points") from "Allostatic Overload" ("expression of
pathophysiology by the chronic over-activation of regulating systems") (p.17). A
direct-comparison slide (p.19), which carries no attribution on the slide itself, states:
"Homeostasis describes mechanisms that HOLD CONSTANT a controlled variable by sensing its
deviation from a 'setpoint' and feeding back to correct the error. Allostasis describes
mechanisms that CHANGE a controlled variable by predicting what level will be needed and
overriding local feedback to meet anticipated demand." The following slide (p.20), credited to
"Bruce McEwen," adds a qualifier the p.19 comparison slide does not carry: "Some systems
operate under the homeostasis model: Thermal Regulation, Oxygen Tension, pH Levels." The

topic: recovery is a planned training means, not an incidental absence of training

---

# "Recovery Is Not Simply a Thing. It Is a Part of a Logically Sequenced Training Plan. Recovery Is a Training Means."

**What it is** - The slide states (U3 L1 p.6, no attribution shown beyond the slide's own
text): "Recovery is not simply a 'thing'. It is [sic, slide reads "apart of"] a part of a
logically sequenced training plan. Recovery is a training means." This follows a slide on
"Preparedness" (p.5) stating: "The best way to increase an athlete's preparedness is to
induce restoration and adaptation by implementing a properly designed periodized training
program that uses logical variations in volume, intensity, and exercise selection. By
including appropriate variation in the training regime, the athlete will have periods of
reduced training volume, reduced training intensity, and complete rest, all of which
dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase the athlete's preparedness to perform at
a high level."

**Why it works** - The slide does not give a physiological mechanism for why planned
recovery periods (as opposed to unplanned or absent recovery) produce better preparedness
beyond restating that they "dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase...
preparedness"; no specific study or data point is cited for this claim in this lecture.
Inference: the practical implication is that recovery periods should be programmed with the
same deliberateness as loading periods (specific volume, intensity, and timing decisions),
rather than treated as simply the days when no training is scheduled.

**When to apply** - As a planning reminder when building a microcycle or mesocycle: recovery
periods should be assigned a specific volume/intensity reduction and a specific purpose
within the plan, not left as a residual default. Eric's baseline: its in-season rule,
"maintain intensity, reduce volume," is itself a deliberate, programmed recovery-adjacent
decision rather than an absence of planning (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`), and its broader statement is that
"recovery has to be earned by training hard first" and that recovery technology is "useful
but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Recovery and sleep," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9`). Inference: both
share the premise that recovery is an active, managed element of a plan, not a passive gap.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a stated principle, not a quantified
prescription; the slide gives no specific formula for how much volume or intensity reduction
constitutes adequate "recovery as a training means" for a given athlete or training phase.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific worked example (a named athlete, phase, or numeric reduction) is
given on this slide.

**Related** - [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (same lecture, the
consequence of not treating recovery this way).
</content>

# "Recovery Is Not Simply a Thing. It Is a Part of a Logically Sequenced Training Plan. Recovery Is a Training Means."

**What it is** - Evans states, in his own words (U3 L1 p.6): "Recovery is not simply a
'thing'. It is a part of a logically sequenced training plan. Recovery is a training means."
This follows a slide on "Preparedness" (p.5) stating: "The best way to increase an athlete's
preparedness is to induce restoration and adaptation by implementing a properly designed
periodized training program that uses logical variations in volume, intensity, and exercise
selection. By including appropriate variation in the training regime, the athlete will have
periods of reduced training volume, reduced training intensity, and complete rest, all of
which dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase the athlete's preparedness to
perform at a high level."

**Why it works** - Evans does not give a physiological mechanism for why planned recovery
periods (as opposed to unplanned or absent recovery) produce better preparedness beyond
restating that they "dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase... preparedness"; no
specific study or data point is cited for this claim in this lecture. Inference: the practical
implication is that recovery periods should be programmed with the same deliberateness as
loading periods (specific volume, intensity, and timing decisions), rather than treated as
simply the days when no training is scheduled.

**When to apply** - As a planning reminder when building a microcycle or mesocycle: recovery
periods should be assigned a specific volume/intensity reduction and a specific purpose within
the plan, not left as a residual default. This is consistent with Eric's baseline's own
in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume," which is itself a deliberate,
programmed recovery-adjacent decision rather than an absence of planning
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`), and with the baseline's broader statement
that "recovery has to be earned by training hard first" and that recovery technology is
"useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Recovery and sleep," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9`) - both share the premise that recovery is an
active, managed element of a plan, not a passive gap.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a stated principle, not a quantified prescription;
the slide gives no specific formula for how much volume or intensity reduction constitutes
adequate "recovery as a training means" for a given athlete or training phase. Confidence is
untested.

given on this slide.

consequence of not treating recovery this way).

# The Overtraining Continuum: Acute Fatigue, Functional and Non-Functional Overreaching, Overtraining

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U3 L1 p.10), titled "Overtraining Continuum," presents a
four-stage progression by increasing training/fatigue and decreasing outcome, with no
individual citation given on this specific slide (the surrounding lecture cites no author by
name for this table): Acute Fatigue (timescale: day(s); outcome: increase in performance);
Overreaching, Functional (FOR) (timescale: days/weeks; outcome: temporary decrease, then
recovery); Overreaching, Nonfunctional (NFOR) (timescale: weeks/months; outcome: decrease or
no change, recovery takes weeks to months); Overtraining (timescale: months to a year+;
outcome: decrease, recovery takes months to a year or more). Functional Overreaching is
further defined (p.12): "Stimulates physiological adaptations, which compensate for
training-related stress. Recovery can take days to weeks depending on the stimulus
magnitude." Nonfunctional Overreaching (p.13): "Occurs when intensified training is continued
and results in the stagnation or decreases in performance that would require longer recovery
times. When NFOR is continued for a long period of time, the athlete will eventually reach a
state of overtraining." Overtraining (p.14): "a process of excessive training & non-training
stressors in high performance athletes that may lead to persistent fatigue, performance
decrements, neuroendocrine changes, alterations in mood states, and frequent illness," most
notably upper-respiratory-tract infections, with "Overtraining Syndrome" defined as "a
neuroendocrine disorder that may result from the process of overtraining."

but does not give the diagnostic criteria for distinguishing one stage from the next in real
time (e.g., what specific performance drop or duration marks the transition from FOR to
NFOR); Evans's own later slide in the same lecture (p.17, see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]) states directly that "a
definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not available," which is consistent with this
continuum being a retrospective classification (assigned after recovery time is observed)
rather than a prospective diagnostic test.

likely sits on a severity/duration spectrum, and for setting expectations about recovery
timescales at each stage. Eric's baseline: it does not use this specific FOR/NFOR/OTS

adopted specifically to catch problems early via objective daily testing rather than through
symptom-based staging (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"

objective) approach to the same underlying underperformance-and-recovery problem this
continuum describes.

sympathetic/parasympathetic types with their own symptom tables (p.15-18); see
[[claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]] for that
material in full. Confidence is untested.

HRV/readiness device screenshots moving from "Complete recovery" toward "Distress /
Exhaustion" and back - a single anecdote, untested, detailed in
[[claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]] rather
than reproduced here.

**Related** - [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]],

# Evans's Own Conclusion: No Definitive Diagnostic Tool for Overtraining Syndrome Exists

**What it is** - After surveying eight "hypothetical mechanisms" of overtraining syndrome
(OTS) across biochemistry, cardiovascular/HRV, immune system, hormonal, brain, training
status, psychometrics, and psychomotor speed (U3 L2 p.2-16), Evans's closing slide (p.17),
titled "Reality and OTS," states in his own words: "Definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not
available. The human organisms of made of up many [sic] biological systems that are
independent and dependent upon each other, and the interaction between them is contextual on
the readiness and preparedness of those systems, the imposed stimuli, and the adaptation path
the individual makes to cope with the stressor. The reliance of adopting sound training theory
principles, and performance monitoring will continue to be paramount to keep athletes
improving in their respective sport." Along the way, he makes several specific claims: on
HRV, "HRV is a great way to assess persons ability to adapt to stressors" (p.9); on hormonal
markers, "hormonal markers are a potent tool to gauge disturbances" (p.12), and "Testosterone
/ Cortisol ratio used to be considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore"
(p.12); on immune markers, "there is NO evidence to low glutamine levels with impaired immune
function" (p.11); on the literature generally, "Research seems to be relatively scarce since
ensuring OTS is difficult... The biggest issue with the literature is the TIME at which they
are studying high level athletes" (p.10).

**Why it works** - This is Evans's own synthesized conclusion after reviewing multiple

# Evans's Framing of the Periodization Evidence Debate: "Classic" Versus "Non-Classic" Literature

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.13-14), titled "Literature Issue," present two
opposing characterizations of the periodization research base, in his own summarizing words.
Non-classic literature (his term for research not from Eastern Europe or the Soviet Union) is
described as: "Suggestive there is little research to support Periodization. Very few elite
athletes are used in the research. Short term studies. One dimensional. Non-classic believes
(most of the time) the CLASSIC literature is promoting linear periodization." Classic
literature is described as: "Large amount of insight to support the usage of a
multidimensional, planned approach. A lot of studies utilizing elite athletes. Long term
studies available." He then quotes L.P. Matveyev directly, dated 1977: "Wave oscillations
characterize load dynamics in both relatively small and more prolonged phases (stages,
periods) or the training process," offered as an example of what the classic literature
argues (a non-linear, "wave" model), in apparent contrast to the non-classic camp's alleged
belief that classic literature promotes strictly linear periodization. The following slide
(p.15) shows "Figure 7: Matveyev's Classic Model of an Annual Training Plan," with red arrows
highlighting the "daily, microcycle, and mesocycle fluctuations" in volume, intensity and
technical training; p.16 then states directly, "Non-linear in CLASSIC literature."

**Why it works** - Evans does not name specific non-classic authors, studies, or a specific
review supporting either characterization; this is his own summary framing of a two-sided
debate, not a mechanism claim. Evans's own position is explicit: classic periodization is
non-linear (p.16), illustrated by Matveyev's model with fluctuations highlighted (p.15).

**When to apply** - As a prompt to ask, when evaluating any periodization claim in this
course, which side of this stated debate it draws from, and whether Evans names specific
studies or only characterizes a camp generally. Eric's baseline: it records an analogous,
independently-arrived-at tension about evidence quality in a different area (subjective
wellness surveys versus objective mRSI monitoring, `method-baseline.md`, tension #3).
Inference: this shares the general pattern of a practitioner weighing which evidence
tradition to trust, though the baseline's specific tension is not about periodization
research.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans names no specific non-classic study or author by
name in this segment, so the "little research," "very few elite athletes," and "short term"
characterizations cannot be checked against a specific citation from this lecture alone; the
same is true of the "classic literature" characterization, apart from the single named
Matveyev 1977 quote and the p.15 figure. Do not treat either side of this debate as settled
based on this slide; it is Evans's summary of a debate, and he does not cite a source
publication for the Matveyev 1977 quote or the p.15 figure beyond the name and year.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The Matveyev 1977 quote and the p.15 "Figure 7" model are the only specific
citations given as examples of "classic" literature's position.

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]] (the "classic" periodization
model Evans goes on to teach in the remainder of this lecture and the next).
</content>

# Periodization's Central Concept Is Variation and Timing, Not Time Itself

**What it is** - Evans states (U3 L4 p.16): "Central concept of periodization: VARIATION.
Planning and programming to achieve an increase in athletic preparedness and to optimize
readiness. The sequence and timing of the application of the training stimulus. It is when
you do what you do. Example: Max strength may be important in the preparation, but in the
wrong place, it can have negative interactions." A following slide (p.19) restates this as:
"The interaction & interdependence of the training components. No training component is in
isolation. Timing NOT time." And (p.20): "To have the team or individual ready to perform at
their optimum at the appointed time."

**Why it works** - Evans does not give a specific mechanism for why a given training
component's placement (rather than its total duration) determines whether it helps or hurts
readiness; the single example given ("Max strength may be important in the preparation, but
in the wrong place, it can have negative interactions") names an outcome (negative
interactions) without specifying which placements are wrong or why. Inference: this connects
to the same training-compatibility idea Eric's baseline documents independently (see below),
where incompatible qualities interfere with each other if trained at full intensity in the
same block - Evans's principle can be read as the more general statement that this kind of
interaction risk exists throughout a plan, not only between simultaneously-trained qualities
but between sequentially-placed ones.

**When to apply** - As a check when building or reviewing a periodized plan: is a given
training emphasis placed at the right point in the sequence relative to competition and to
other training components, not merely present for enough total time? Eric's baseline: its
training-compatibility constraint states that "incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal
strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the
same block... 'you can't ride two horses with one saddle'" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`), and its residual-effects based retraining
cadence is aerobic capacity and max strength re-exposed roughly every 30 days, speed roughly
every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, same section). Inference: this is closely consistent with
Evans's principle here, since both are timing-based rather than pure-duration-based planning
rules.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a stated planning philosophy, not a specific
sequencing rule; the slide does not say which training components interact negatively with
which others, or by how much, so it cannot be applied as a checklist without the more specific
compatibility material Eric's baseline documents (which itself, per that baseline's own
tension log, is Inferred course-team material, not confirmed as Eric's individually-authored
position). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The only example given is the general "max strength in the wrong place" case
described above, without specifics.

**Related** - [[claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]],
[[framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities]] (a more detailed,
later treatment of sequencing versus simultaneous training of biomotor qualities).
</content>

# Bill Sands's "Performance Garden": Training Plans [sic] Seeds, Rest Lets Them Grow, Judgment Lets Them Bear Fruit

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U3 L4 p.21) credits "Bill Sands, Performance Garden" with a
three-part metaphor: "Training - Plan seeds. Rest/Recovery - Allow plants to grow. With
Intelligence & Common Sense - Allow Plants to Bear Fruit." (The slide reads "Training - Plan
seeds"; "Plan" is probably a typo for "Plant" given the surrounding garden imagery, but the
slide is not corrected here since the intended word cannot be confirmed.) No further citation
(publication, year, or context) is given for this metaphor beyond the named source.

**Why it works** - This is an explicitly metaphorical framing, not a mechanism claim; the
slide gives no biological or training-science content beyond the analogy itself. Inference:
the three-part structure maps training to input (planting), recovery to a necessary
maturation period the coach cannot rush (growth), and coaching judgment to the factor that
converts potential into realized result (fruit) - paralleling the course's broader theme
(seen also in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]] and
[[principle--recovery-is-a-training-means]]) that recovery is an active, necessary phase, not

# Bompa's Three Annual-Plan Cycle Types: Monocycle, Bicycle, Tricycle

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.25-30, repeated identically in U3 L5 p.3-8), cited
throughout to "Bompa, 2009," present three annual-plan structures. Monocycle: "Only ONE
competition phase and one major peak," recommended "FOR NOVICE AND JUNIOR ATHLETES. LONG
PREPARATORY PHASE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TECHNICAL/TACTICAL/PHYSICAL DOMAINS," with a
stated week distribution per 52-week cycle: Preparatory >= 32 weeks, Competitive 10-15 weeks,
Transition 5 weeks. Bicycle: "TWO competition phases and two major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR
ELITE ATHLETES WHO QUALIFY FOR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS. TRY TO KEEP THE PREPARATORY PHASES AS
LONG AS POSSIBLE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT," distribution per 26-week cycle: Preparatory 13 weeks,
Competitive 5-10 weeks, Transition 3 weeks. Tricycle: "THREE competition phases and three
major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR INTERNATIONAL-LEVEL ATHLETES. SOLID FOUNDATION IS INSTALLED AND
THEY CAN TOLERATE MULTIPLE PEAKS. 3 OR MORE," distribution per 17-18-week cycle: Preparatory
>= 8 weeks, Competitive 3-5 weeks, Transition 2-3 weeks. No book title beyond "Bompa" and the
year 2009 is given on the slides.

**Why it works** - The slides state the recommended athlete level and week distribution for
each cycle type but do not explain the physiological reasoning for why, for example, a
tricycle's shorter preparatory phase (>=8 weeks versus a monocycle's >=32) is appropriate only
for athletes who already have "a solid foundation... installed." The slides give no mechanism.
Inference: a trained athlete needing less time to re-establish base qualities before
specializing toward a peak is implied by the athlete-level guideline but not stated
explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** - As a first-pass structural choice when designing an annual plan: how many
distinct peaks does the competition calendar actually require, and does the athlete's training
age support the correspondingly shorter preparatory phases of a multi-cycle plan? Evans's own
U3 L7 p.5 (Step Three, "Setup Periodization Model") offers "Single / Double / Triple
Periodization, Team Sport considerations" as a direct menu choice, showing the course links
this cycle-type framework into the ten-step annual-plan process (see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]), even though the worked
wide-receiver example does not name which of the three it uses. Eric's baseline: its own
annual-plan language treats the plan as "a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract," built
around "the competition calendar, key non-training dates... and phase-by-phase volume/
intensity waves" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23`) without naming a specific monocycle/bicycle/
tricycle choice. Inference: this framework gives that flexible planning language a specific
named structural menu to choose from; for a sport like college football, with a single
primary competitive season, this framework's monocycle category (long preparatory phase, one
major peak window covering the season) is the closest fit among the three named here.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No book title, edition, or page number is given beyond
"Bompa, 2009," so these week-distribution figures cannot be verified against a primary source
within this ingest; the `periodization--bompa` book already staged in this library's vault
does not, based on its file listing reviewed for this ingest's dedup check, include an entry
titled around monocycle/bicycle/tricycle annual-plan types specifically (its files cover
LTAD, step loading, training effects, supercompensation, and general periodization
principles instead), so this is recorded as a distinct, not-yet-cross-checked secondary
citation. Do not apply these week counts rigidly to a sport whose season length does not match
the 52/26/17-18-week cycle lengths given (a college football season, for example, does not map

stated week distribution per 52-week cycle: Preparatory >= 32 weeks, Competitive 10-15 weeks,

ELITE ATHLETES WHO QUALIFY FOR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS. TRY TO KEEP THE PREPARATORY PHASES AS
LONG AS POSSIBLE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT," distribution per 26-week cycle: Preparatory 13 weeks,
Competitive 5-10 weeks, Transition 3 weeks. Tricycle: "THREE competition phases and three
major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR INTERNATIONAL-LEVEL ATHLETES. SOLID FOUNDATION IS INSTALLED AND
THEY CAN TOLERATE MULTIPLE PEAKS. 3 OR MORE," distribution per 17-18-week cycle: Preparatory

year 2009 is given on the slides.

each cycle type but do not explain the physiological reasoning for why, for example, a

implied by the athlete-level guideline but not stated explicitly on these slides.
