# Bompa's Macrocycle Phases and Their Stated Objectives: Preparatory, Competitive, Unloading/Tapering, Transition

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.15-19), cited to "Bompa, 2009," list a macrocycle's
phases (Preparatory, split into General and Specific/Special; Competitive, split into
Pre-competitive and Main Competitive; Unloading/Tapering; Transition) with stated objectives
for each. Preparatory: "ACQUIRE AND IMPROVE GENERAL PHYSICAL TRAINING CAPACITY, IMPROVE THE
BIOMOTOR ABILITIES REQUIRED BY THE SPORT, CULTIVATE PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, DEVELOP, IMPROVE,
PERFECT TECHNICAL ELEMENTS, FAMILIARIZE ATHLETES WITH THE BASIC STRATEGIC MANEUVERS MASTERED
IN THE FOLLOWING PHASES, TEACH ATHLETES THE THEORY AND METHODOLOGY OF TRAINING SPECIFIC TO THE
SPORT." Competitive: "CONTINUED IMPROVEMENT OR MAINTENANCE OF SPORT-SPECIFIC BIOMOTOR
ABILITIES, ENHANCING PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, PERFECTING AND CONSOLIDATING TECHNIQUE, ELEVATING
PERFORMANCE TO THE HIGHEST LEVEL, DISSIPATING FATIGUE AND ELEVATING PREPAREDNESS, PERFECTING
TECHNICAL AND TACTICAL MANEUVERS, GAINING COMPETITIVE EXPERIENCE, MAINTAINING SPORT-SPECIFIC
FITNESS." Unloading/Tapering: "BEST WAY TO ELEVATE THE ATHLETE'S PREPAREDNESS AND STIMULATE A
SUPERCOMPENSATION OF PERFORMANCE THAT WILL INCREASE THE ATHLETE'S PERFORMANCE POTENTIAL DURING
THE COMPETITION," lasting "1-2 WEEKS." Transition: "FACILITATES PSYCHOLOGICAL REST,
RELAXATION, BIOLOGICAL REGENERATION, MAINTAINING AN ACCEPTABLE LEVEL OF GENERAL PHYSICAL
PREPARATION (40-50% OF COMPETITIVE PHASE)," associated with "DETRAINING." A separate slide
(p.20) pairs Transition with a Bompa detraining table distinguishing short-term detraining
(under 4 weeks) from long-term detraining (over 4 weeks), without further detail on the pages
read for this ingest.

this specific ordering (general preparatory work before specific, tapering immediately before
competition, detraining-permissive transition after) produces better outcomes than an

sport-specificity, peak, then allow planned detraining before the next cycle) is implied by
the sequence itself but not argued for explicitly on these slides.

cycle types from [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]. Eric's baseline: it

`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21`). Inference: this Evans framework gives that
baseline sequence a named phase-objective structure (General Preparatory versus Specific
Preparatory, Pre-competitive versus Main Competitive) that the baseline material does not
spell out at this level of detail.

is given beyond "Bompa, 2009," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this
ingest, and the vault's `periodization--bompa` book does not, per its current file listing,
stage an entry matching this specific phase-objective breakdown. The Transition phase's "40-50%
of competitive phase" general-physical-preparation figure is stated without explaining what
baseline value that percentage is taken from (percentage of the competitive phase's volume?
intensity? Both are plausible readings and the slide does not disambiguate). Confidence is
untested.

**Example** - No sport-specific worked example is given on these slides.

[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Step Four of Evans's own later
process, "Setup Training Phases," names this same phase list directly).
</content>

# Evans's Ten-Step Process for Building an Annual Plan (American Football Wide Receiver Example)

**What it is** - Evans presents a ten-step sequence for building an annual plan (U3 L7),
applied throughout to "Sport: American Football, Position: Wide Receiver" (p.2). Step One,
"Build Profile": a table of System, Notes, and Rationale covering Autonomic NS
(parasympathetic dominance, for "fast recovery abilities, resiliency"), Central NS (high
central drive, for "speed of movement, reaction time, tactical decision making"),
Neuromuscular (large fast-twitch percentage especially lower body, large concentric/eccentric
loading, for "speed of movement, deceleration qualities"), Energy Supply Systems (per
time-motion analysis: alactic and aerobic capacity), Common Injuries (ankle, knee, hip,
shoulder, fingers, informing "exercise prescription, loading strategies"), and
Anthropometrics (low body fat percent, moderate cross-sectional area for force production and
collisions). Step Two: "Setup Calendar" (competitions, travel, intensive practice periods,
organizational dates, holidays, training camps/facilities). Step Three: "Setup Periodization
Model" (single/double/triple periodization, team-sport considerations - the same
monocycle/bicycle/tricycle menu named in
[[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]], though this lecture does not say which one the
wide-receiver example uses). Step Four: "Setup Training Phases" (Preparatory-General/Specific,
Competition-Precompetitive/Main, Unloading/Tapering, Transition - see
[[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]]). Step Five: "Setup Bioenergetic Sequence"
(per athlete profile/TMA; aerobic, anaerobic-glycolytic, anaerobic-alactic; power vs.
capacity, time to develop, developmental potential). Step Six: "Setup Biodynamic Sequence"
(per profile, periodization model, phases, bioenergetics; exercises classified
GPE/SPE/SDE/Competitive - a classification already staged in this library's primary-source
Bondarchuk entries, not re-atomized here). Step Seven: "Setup Biomotor Sequence" (strength,
speed, endurance, flexibility/mobility, skill; e.g. "Maximal-strength SPE vs SDE," "Alactic
capacity SPE vs SDE"). Step Eight: "Setup Mesocycles and Microcycles" (calendar-driven
duration; loading strategies - Step, Wave, Flat; mesocycle dominant themes -
Primary/Secondary/Tertiary; Complex vs. Sequential sequencing; days per week; facilities).
Step Nine: "Setup Workouts within Microcycles" (U3 L7 p.11; mesocycle theme; microcycle type -
"What type of microcycle am I needing? Adjustment, Loading, Impact, etc." - the same six
named types Issurin (2008) gives, staged from the primary source at
`block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md`; key-workout
placement and sequencing follow the same primary source's
`heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules.md`; supplemental workouts). Step Ten:
"Setup Assessment & Monitoring" (assessments; monitoring frequency - Daily, X per Week,
Biweekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Yearly). The lecture closes with a single unelaborated slide,
"SLEEP ON IT" (p.13).

**Why it works** - Evans does not state why this specific ten-step order (profile before
calendar, calendar before periodization model, bioenergetics before biodynamics before
biomotor) is necessary rather than some other sequence. Inference: the order appears designed
so that each step's output becomes an input constraint for the next (the athlete's profile and
the competition calendar constrain which periodization model and phases are feasible, which in
turn constrain the bioenergetic, biodynamic, and biomotor sequencing choices, which in turn
determine mesocycle and microcycle and workout design, with assessment and monitoring set up
last to track the resulting plan) - but Evans does not argue for this dependency structure
explicitly in the lecture; it is read from the sequence itself.

**When to apply** - As a step-by-step checklist when building any annual plan from scratch, for
football or another sport, ensuring the athlete profile and calendar constraints are
established before periodization, phase, and sequencing decisions are made. Eric's baseline:
it does not document an equivalent explicit ten-step process; its closest parallel is the
department's own three-phase Playbook Development Plan roadmap (Foundation, Operational
Depth, Education and Culture, `method-baseline.md`, "Department model and roles"), which
operates at the departmental-documentation level rather than the individual-athlete
annual-plan level this framework addresses. Inference: this framework's Step One profile
table (ANS, CNS, neuromuscular, energy systems, injuries, anthropometrics) is a more granular
starting-point checklist than anything named in the baseline's testing and assessment
material.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This entire ten-step sequence is applied only to a
hypothetical, illustrative "American Football, Wide Receiver" profile, not to a named real
athlete; the Step One profile values (parasympathetic dominance, large fast-twitch
percentage, low body fat) are stated as generic assumptions about "a wide receiver" as a
position archetype, not as measured data from any specific player. Do not treat this as a
validated planning method; it demonstrates Evans's own applied teaching sequence, and no
outcome data (whether a plan built this way produced better results than an alternative
sequence) is given anywhere in this lecture. Confidence is untested. The Step Six exercise
classification (GPE/SPE/SDE/CE) is not re-atomized as its own entry here because it
duplicates primary-source content already staged at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`.

**Example** - The entire lecture is the worked example: a football wide receiver's Step One
profile, described above, carried through all ten steps. The continuation into a specific
weekly loading template appears in the next lecture; see
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]].

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]],
[[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]],
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]]. Step Nine (U3 L7
p.11) asks which Issurin microcycle type is needed; see
`block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md` and
`block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules.md` for
the primary-source six-type table and six-step sequence (this entry's own former
`framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps.md` staging-book duplicate of those
two files was deleted at review; see `fixes_evans_applied.md`).
</content>

Tapering, Transition - see [[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]]). Step Five:
"Setup Bioenergetic Sequence" (per athlete profile/TMA; aerobic, anaerobic-glycolytic,
anaerobic-alactic; power vs. capacity, time to develop, developmental potential). Step Six:
"Setup Biodynamic Sequence" (per profile, periodization model, phases, bioenergetics;
exercises classified GPE/SPE/SDE/Competitive - a classification already staged in this
library's primary-source Bondarchuk entries, not re-atomized here). Step Seven: "Setup
Biomotor Sequence" (strength, speed, endurance, flexibility/mobility, skill; e.g. "Maximal
-strength SPE vs SDE," "Alactic capacity SPE vs SDE"). Step Eight: "Setup Mesocycles and
Microcycles" (calendar-driven duration; loading strategies - Step, Wave, Flat; mesocycle
dominant themes - Primary/Secondary/Tertiary; Complex vs. Sequential sequencing; days per
week; facilities). Step Nine: "Setup Workouts within Microcycles" (mesocycle theme; microcycle
type per [[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]]; key-workout placement;
supplemental workouts). Step Ten: "Setup Assessment & Monitoring" (assessments; monitoring
frequency - Daily, X per Week, Biweekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Yearly). The lecture closes with
a single unelaborated slide, "SLEEP ON IT" (p.13).

**Why it works** - Evans does not state why this specific ten-step order (profile before
calendar, calendar before periodization model, bioenergetics before biodynamics before
biomotor) is necessary rather than some other sequence; Inference: the order appears designed
so that each step's output becomes an input constraint for the next (the athlete's profile and
the competition calendar constrain which periodization model and phases are feasible, which in
turn constrain the bioenergetic, biodynamic, and biomotor sequencing choices, which in turn
determine mesocycle and microcycle and workout design, with assessment and monitoring set up
last to track the resulting plan) - but Evans does not argue for this dependency structure
explicitly in the lecture; it is read from the sequence itself.

**When to apply** - As a step-by-step checklist when building any annual plan from scratch, for
football or another sport, ensuring the athlete profile and calendar constraints are
established before periodization, phase, and sequencing decisions are made. Eric's baseline
does not document an equivalent explicit ten-step process; its closest parallel is the
department's own three-phase Playbook Development Plan roadmap (Foundation, Operational
Depth, Education and Culture, `method-baseline.md`, "Department model and roles"), which
operates at the departmental-documentation level rather than the individual-athlete
annual-plan level this framework addresses. This framework's Step One profile table (ANS,
CNS, neuromuscular, energy systems, injuries, anthropometrics) is a more granular
starting-point checklist than anything named in the baseline's testing and assessment
material.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This entire ten-step sequence is applied only to a
hypothetical, illustrative "American Football, Wide Receiver" profile, not to a named real
athlete; the Step One profile values (parasympathetic dominance, large fast-twitch
percentage, low body fat) are stated as generic assumptions about "a wide receiver" as a
position archetype, not as measured data from any specific player. Do not treat this as a
validated planning method; it demonstrates Evans's own applied teaching sequence, and no
outcome data (whether a plan built this way produced better results than an alternative
sequence) is given anywhere in this lecture. Confidence is untested. The Step Six exercise
classification (GPE/SPE/SDE/CE) is not re-atomized as its own entry here because it
duplicates primary-source content already staged at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`.

**Example** - The entire lecture is the worked example: a football wide receiver's Step One
profile, described above, carried through all ten steps. The continuation into a specific
weekly loading template appears in the next lecture; see
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]].

[[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]],
[[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]],
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]].

# Buzzichelli's Integration and Development Models: Complex Versus Sequential Biomotor Training

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.26-30), cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011," present a
"Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities" framework with two named components relevant
to this entry. Integration: "the way motor capacity is trained in the annual plan; in
relation to the others," with two options: "Complex" ("Biomotor Abilities Are All Trained At
The Same Time") or "Sequential" ("Biomotor Abilities Are Emphasized At Different Times During
The Annual Plan"). Development: "the way each conditional motor capacity is trained during
the annual plan," with three named patterns: Complex development, illustrated at three
timescales - within a training unit ("MxS, Power, Muscular Endurance are trained within this
sequence within a single training session"), within a microcycle ("MxS, Power, ME are all
trained in the microcycle in different training workouts"), and within a mesocycle ("MxS,
Power, ME are trained throughout the mesocycle, during dedicated microcycles"); Sequential
development, distinguishing "Immediate Realization" ("At the end of the mesocycle, the
indexes of the trained biomotor quality are improved") from "Delayed Realization" ("At the
end of the mesocycle, the indexes... are depressed but improve later"); and Pendular
development ("Two qualities of biomotor abilities are trained in alternative fashion (e.g.,
Max Strength followed by Power followed by Max Strength followed by Power)"). No book title is
given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** - The slides name the integration and development options and give brief
illustrative examples (MxS/Power/ME sequencing; the delayed-realization pattern) but do not
state the physiological mechanism for why a given quality shows delayed rather than immediate
realization; this is presented as a descriptive taxonomy of observed or theorized patterns,
not a derived model.

**When to apply** - As vocabulary for describing how a program is choosing to combine
multiple biomotor qualities: are strength, power, and endurance work happening together
(complex) or in separate blocks (sequential), and within complex training, at what
timescale (session, microcycle, or mesocycle) is that combination happening? Eric's baseline:
its training-compatibility constraint states that incompatible qualities are not trained
together at full intensity, compatible ones are trained together, and the rest at a retention
dose (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`). Inference: this is effectively a rule for
choosing between this framework's Complex and Sequential integration options based on quality
compatibility, though the baseline material does not use Buzzichelli's specific vocabulary.
Eric's baseline's own delayed-transformation awareness (a 30-day residual-effect retraining
cadence for strength) is also consistent with, though not identical to, this framework's
"Delayed Realization" concept.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No page number or book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli,
2011," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this ingest; this entry
should be treated as Evans's slide transcription of a secondary citation, not a confirmed
quotation. Inference: the slide gives no criteria for predicting, in advance, whether two
given qualities will show immediate or delayed realization when trained together - this can
apparently only be observed after the fact. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The MxS/Power/Muscular-Endurance sequencing example given at the training-unit,
microcycle, and mesocycle timescales, described above, is the lecture's only worked
illustration, and it is generic (no specific sets, reps, or athlete given).

**Related** - [[framework--buzzichelli-load-progression-and-specificity-continuum]] (the
companion Load Progression and Specificity components of the same Buzzichelli, 2011
framework), [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].
</content>

# Buzzichelli's Load Progression (Wave Loading) and Specificity Continuum (Complex Versus Sequential Training Means)

**What it is** - Continuing the same "Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities"
framework cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011" (U3 L5 p.26, see also
[[framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities]]), two further
components are given, each an image slide with a bar chart. Load Progression, "WAVE LOADING"
(p.31), titled "Load within the mesocycle / Load within the microcycle": a four-panel bar
chart (Micro 1-4 on a 0-6 scale, read from the chart) for four loading patterns - Ascending
Ond.: Micro1 4, Micro2 3, Micro3 5, Micro4 2.5; Descending Ond.: Micro1 5, Micro2 3, Micro3 4,
Micro4 2.5; Step Loading: Micro1 3, Micro2 4, Micro3 5, Micro4 2.5; Flat Loading: Micro1-3
roughly 4.5 each, Micro4 2.5. Load Progression in a Competitive Microcycle (Weekly Match)
(p.32): a seven-day bar chart (0-120 scale, read from the chart) - Mon 50, Tue 85, Wed 100,
Thu 85, Fri 55, Sat 55, Sun 100. Specificity of the Training Means (p.33): a two-way
distinction between "Complex" ("General And Specific Training Means Are Utilized At The Same
Time") and "Sequential" ("General Training Means Precede Specific Training Means"), each
illustrated with its own annual-plan-style bar/line chart but no further numeric labels. No
book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** - The p.31 chart names "wave loading" and gives four patterns (Ascending
Ond., Descending Ond., Step Loading, Flat Loading) at two timescales without stating a
mechanism for why a wave pattern (as opposed to, for example, a linear pattern; see the
vault's Bompa `framework--step-loading-paradigm.md` for a different named loading scheme) is
preferred at either the mesocycle or microcycle level. The Specificity distinction states
that general training means can either precede specific ones (Sequential) or run
concurrently (Complex), which mirrors the same general-to-specific structure found in
Bondarchuk's GPE/SPE/SDE/CE exercise-class continuum (already staged in this library at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`),
though Evans's slide does not explicitly connect the two.

**When to apply** - As a two-question check when programming a training block: is the load
progression across the mesocycle or microcycle following a deliberate wave pattern (rather
than, implicitly, a flat or purely linear one), and are general and specific training means
being run concurrently or in sequence? Eric's baseline: its own preferred model is

# "Body Composition Analysis Is NOT a Measurement, It Is a Prediction"

**What it is** - Evans states directly (U3 L6 p.6, slide titled "Body Composition Reality"):
"Body composition analysis is NOT a measurement, it is a PREDICTION. Want to get a true
measurement of body fat? Carcass Analysis... so you're telling me I have to be dead to get my
body fat measured?" (paraphrased rhetorical framing, quoted as close to the slide's own
phrasing as its sparse text allows). The following slides (p.7-9) list body-composition models
(Two, Three, and Four Compartment) and the most widely used field methods (Hydrostatic
Weighing, BodPod, DEXA, Bioelectrical Impedance, Skinfolds). The p.9 error-rate slide is laid
out in three blocks: "Small Error Rates for Populations" - Underwater Weighing (UW) 0.1-2.1%,
BodPod (BP) 2%, Skinfolds (SF) 6%, DEXA 1-2%, alongside a separate list of population-level
error sources ("Ethnicity, Age, Gender..."); "Large Error Rates for Individuals" - UW 5%+, BP
6%+, Bioelectrical Impedance (BIA) 8-9% (BIA has no population-level figure; 8-9% is its only
figure on this slide), Skinfolds 10-15%, DEXA 4-10%; and, set apart under its own heading,
"Tracking over time... different? SF: 3-5%."

**Why it works** - Evans's own reasoning is that only carcass analysis (necessarily
post-mortem) directly measures body fat, so every practical field method is instead a
statistical prediction from indirect proxies; this is a stated epistemic point about
measurement validity, not a physiological mechanism claim. Inference: the practical
implication is that population-level error rates (the more favorable numbers in the table)
should not be mistaken for individual-athlete accuracy, since the same slide explicitly
separates population from individual error and reports individual-level error as higher for
every method that has both figures (BIA has only the individual-level figure, so no
within-method comparison is possible for it).

**When to apply** - As a caution when reporting or discussing body-composition numbers with
coaches or athletes: treat any single body-fat percentage as an estimate with a real
error margin, not a precise fact, and prefer within-method, within-device tracking over time
(the slide's own separate skinfolds figure, 3-5% under "Tracking over time," supports
within-method tracking) over comparing absolute numbers across different measurement methods.
Eric's baseline: DEXA and body-composition assessment are owned by Performance Nutrition, not
Applied Performance, with body-composition testing capped at four times per year
(`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition," citing
`ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`). Inference: this is consistent with treating
body-composition testing as a lower-frequency, imprecise-instrument measure rather than a
high-frequency precise one.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide gives a separate, lower skinfold figure (3-5%)
for tracking change over time, distinct from its 6% population and 10-15% individual figures;
this supports within-method tracking rather than indicating an unreconciled inconsistency. No
citation year or source is given for the compiled error-rate table itself, so its provenance
cannot be verified from this lecture. The p.9 slide also lists Ethnicity, Age, and Gender as
error sources without further elaboration. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The error-rate table itself, described above, is the lecture's worked
illustration; no specific athlete case is given.

**Related** - None found elsewhere in this library specifically comparing body-composition
method error rates at population versus individual level (checked by grep for "DEXA" and
"body composition" combined with "error rate").
</content>

# Build the Testing Battery Around a Test-Order Protocol and Sport-Specific Rationale, Not a Generic Checklist

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L6) give two related pieces. First, "Assessment
Considerations" (p.3): Athlete Preparation (diet, training, testing), Test Environment
(surface, cleanliness, temperature, time of day), Test Order ("Non Physical -> Physical (High
Velocity -> Low Velocity)"), and an Equipment Checklist & Assignments (per drill/activity:
equipment required, test procedures, who is in charge of testing and data collection). Second,
three worked sport-specific battery tables, each with a Test and a stated Rationale column
(p.20-22): for Track Cyclists in a velodrome - Anthropometry (assess body composition), VO2Max
("Cyclists on Track are often characterized with high aerobic power"), Alactic Peak Power, 6s
("Examine the alactic power mechanism specific in the leg musculature"), 30-min Time Trial
("'Race of Truth'. No tactics involved (drafting)"), Movement Screen; for Basketball -
Anthropometry (assess and compare against positional values), Vertical Jump ("common feature
in offensive and defensive movements"), Sprints 5/10/20m (acceleration and speed), Right/Left
Shuffle Line-to-Line Drill (anaerobic-glycolytic capacity), Yo-Yo Intermittent Test (aerobic
capacity), 1-6RM Squat/Bench (maximal contractile qualities), Movement Screen; for Rowers -
Anthropometry, a 7x4-min Incremental Test based on best 2000m time (submaximal capacity,
efficiency, and training zones from lactate and HR data), 1-6RM Squat/Bench Pull/Clean
(maximal strength qualities), Movement Screen.

**Why it works** - The test-order rule (non-physical before physical, high-velocity before
low-velocity) is stated without an explicit mechanism on this slide, though the general logic
in sport-science practice (not stated by Evans here) is that fatigue from a low-velocity or
high-fatigue test can degrade performance on a subsequent high-velocity test if the order is
reversed; this is Inference, not something the slide itself explains. The three sport-battery
tables each pair a test to a stated rationale tied to that sport's specific demands (aerobic
power for track cycling's sustained efforts, vertical jump for basketball's offensive/
defensive movements, a 2000m-based incremental test for rowing's specific event distance),
demonstrating the general principle that test selection should follow from event-specific
demands rather than a single universal battery.

**When to apply** - As a template for building any sport's testing battery: state the
rationale for each test in terms of that sport's specific demands, and sequence tests
non-physical-to-physical and high-velocity-to-low-velocity within a session. Eric's baseline:
it independently documents an equivalent sport-specific battery approach at Baylor: "The
Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen,
anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength
endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather
than testing every sport the same way" (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`). Inference: this is the same underlying
principle (sport-specific battery, not one-size-fits-all) that Evans's three worked examples
illustrate, though neither source's specific test list matches the other's exactly (Baylor's
V4 table is not reproduced in Eric's baseline in enough detail to compare test-by-test
against Evans's track-cyclist, basketball, and rower examples).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - These three battery examples are for track cycling,
basketball, and rowing specifically; none is football, so none can be directly copied for a
Baylor football application without independent sport-specific reasoning. The test-order
rationale (non-physical before physical, high-velocity before low-velocity) is stated as a
rule without a cited source or exception cases (e.g., whether a movement screen, arguably
"non-physical" in intensity but requiring some physical performance, fits cleanly into this
binary). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The three sport-battery tables (track cyclist, basketball, rower) described
above are the lecture's worked examples.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Step Ten of that
process, "Setup Assessment & Monitoring," names testing frequency without this level of

# Worked Example: A Wide Receiver's Preparatory-Phase Weekly Loading Template

**What it is** - Continuing the hypothetical "American Football, Wide Receiver" annual-plan
example from U3 L7 (see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]), Evans's slide (U3 L8 p.2) first
gives the phase's content plan by sub-phase: Exercises (GPE & SPE - General; GPE & SPE & SDE -
Specific); Energetics (Alactic Power & Aerobic Capacity - General; Alactic Capacity*, Alactic
Power* & Aerobic Capacity - Specific); Biomotor, General sub-phase (Primary: Flexibility/
Mobility & Muscular Endurance; Secondary: Speed [acceleration qualities], Maximal Strength
[accumulation weights]; Tertiary: Skill) and Specific sub-phase (Primary: Maximal Strength
[lineman, possibly Wide Receiver], Speed [acceleration, longer distances for WR]; Secondary:
Muscular endurance [via weights, running drills, etc], Skill; Tertiary: Flexibility/
Mobility). He then gives a specific weekly structure for two preparatory sub-phases.
Preparatory I, General (p.3-4, 11-12): duration 4-5 weeks, training days Monday/Tuesday/
Thursday/Friday, 8 hours per week ("CARA" - Countable Athletically Related Activities), indoor
turf and weight room available at all times; loading by day - Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off
(Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday Substantial-Large, Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large;
session focus - Monday/Thursday "Aerobic Capacity / UB Focus" (extensive runs, upper body
weights, extensive medicine-ball throws, torso work), Tuesday/Friday "Alactic Power / LB
Focus" (sprints, jumps, intensive medicine-ball throws, lower body weights). Preparatory I,
Specific (p.13-16): duration 3-4 weeks, same weekly structure and facilities, loading by day -
Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off (Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday "Substantial-Large/Extreme,"
Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large; session focus unchanged (Monday/Thursday Aerobic
Capacity/UB with "Extensive Runs/Drills" replacing plain "Extensive Runs," Tuesday/Friday
Alactic Power/LB with "Sprints/Drills" replacing plain "Sprints").

The reference material behind this template sits on five image slides (p.5-10). p.5, "High
Intensity Training Components" (velocity-by-distance curve plus a table of exercise types by
distance band: Strength, Power, Power-Speed, Speed [Elastic Power], Special Endurance). p.6,
"High Intensity Training For Sports," reprints the same distance chart with sport-by-sport
high-intensity distance bars read off the chart: 200m Sprinter to about 200m, 100m Sprinter to
about 100m, Soccer Player to about 90m, Hockey Player to about 60m, "Football Player - Back"
to about 65m, Basketball Player to about 50m, "Football Player - Line" to about 35m, Thrower
to about 25m, Olympic Lifter to about 15m (note the chart says "Back," not "wide receiver," so
this is a position-group figure, not WR-specific). p.7, "Motor Unit Involvement," a bar chart
of approximate percentage of an athlete's total motor units by exercise, from 100% (Clean &
Jerk / Maximal Sprints) down to 5% (Seated Row / Isolated Supplementary Lifts). p.8,
"Training Zones of Physical Capacity," a five-zone table (purpose, magnitude, training method,
energetics, HR, lactate) credited "Borilkievich, V. Physical capacity in extreme muscle
conditions. Leningrad, USSR, 1982." p.9, a Jovanovic/Prilepin effort-level and reps/sets/volume
chart credited "Copyright 2013 by Mladen Jovanovic." p.10, an energy-system work:rest table
(type, intensity, duration, rest interval, number of sets, across alactic and glycolytic power
and capacity and aerobic power and capacity) with no sport or author label on the slide.

**Why it works** - Evans does not explain why this specific day-of-week loading pattern
(Tuesday and Friday as the two highest-load days, bracketing a Medium Monday and Thursday,
with three low/off days) was chosen over an alternative arrangement, nor why the General
sub-phase's 4-5 weeks shortens to 3-4 weeks in the Specific sub-phase; Inference: the
alactic-power/lower-body Tuesday-Friday pairing and aerobic-capacity/upper-body
Monday-Thursday pairing appears designed to separate the two energy-system emphases named in
the Step Five bioenergetic sequence (alactic and aerobic, see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]) onto different training days
rather than combining them in the same session, consistent with the general
training-compatibility logic in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]], but this
specific rationale is not stated by Evans in this lecture.

**When to apply** - As a concrete template for how a general-to-specific preparatory
progression can be laid out week-to-week for a skill-position football athlete, separating
aerobic-capacity/upper-body work from alactic-power/lower-body work by day. Eric's baseline
does not include a comparably detailed weekly loading template for any specific position.
`_book.md` records this course's Exam 3 Study Guide as cited once, for this entry, items 62
and 64-65 (see `_book.md` for the reconciliation); item 62 ("Alactic power speed distance
comparison between offensive lineman vs wide receiver") and items 64-65 (SPE/SDE lower-body
exercise choices for a wide receiver) confirm Evans intended a lineman-versus-wide-receiver
comparison as a further teaching point, but the specific comparative numbers for that
lineman/WR pairing were not found on the slide pages read for this ingest; the closest
figures actually on the slides are the p.6 "Back" versus "Line" position-group bars above, not
a lineman-versus-WR pairing.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is an illustrative teaching template for a
hypothetical wide receiver, not data from any real athlete, team, or season; no actual
performance outcomes, injury data, or adherence data are given anywhere in this lecture to
support that this specific loading pattern is effective. The "8 hours per week (CARA)" and
NCAA-specific facility-availability framing tie this template to US college athletics
countable-hours rules, which Evans references elsewhere in the course as a real constraint
("NCAA reality? CARA hours..." U3 L3 p.12, p.16) but does not re-explain in this lecture; a
reader unfamiliar with NCAA countable-athletically-related-activity rules should not assume
this 8-hour figure applies outside that specific regulatory context. "CARA" itself is not
expanded on this slide; Inference (NCAA term): Countable Athletically Related Activities is
the entry writer's outside expansion of the acronym, not stated by Evans on this slide.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The weekly template itself, described above, plus the p.5-10 reference slides
(distance-by-intensity curve and sport bars, motor-unit-involvement chart, Borilkievich zones,
Jovanovic/Prilepin chart, energy-system work:rest table), is the example.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]],
[[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].
</content>

# A Monitoring Toolkit Organized by Domain, with Named Tools, Frequency, and Relative Cost

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U4 L1 p.16-19) organize monitoring tools into four domains,
each with named solutions and a suggested frequency, and (for two of the four) a relative cost
tier ($ = Low/None, $$ = Moderate, $$$ = High). Nutrition/Body Composition: Bodyweight
(weekly), Skinfolds (biweekly or monthly), Body Comp Analyzers - DEXA, Hydrostatic, InBody,
BodPod (no more than 4x per year), Blood Biomarkers via a sports medicine hospital or LabCorp
(3-4x per year, "focus on simple biomarkers, e.g. serum ferritin, D3"), with a stated minimum
of "Performance metrics + Body Composition," and no cost tier given for this domain.
Psychological: Profile of Mood States (monthly, $), Recovery-Stress Questionnaire for Athletes
(weekly, $), Daily Analysis of Life Demands for Athletes (weekly, $), Smith Relaxation States
Inventory (weekly, $), sRPE "used to calculate training load, monotony, strain" (daily, $), a
custom soreness/sickness/lethargy questionnaire (daily-weekly, $) - all marked for team-sport
use with checkmarks or "Best Athletes" only. Movement/Muscle: FMS, PCA, isolated muscle
testing (e.g. groin squeeze), isolated joint ROM (e.g. total arc) - "Full screen during
critical times, individual tests more frequently," no cost tier given. Physical Fitness: Jump
Tests (Bosco, DJ-RSI, SJ, CMJ, "ES or 2x," $), Sprint Tests 10-20yds (1x, $), Weight Exercises
via Linear Transducers (1-2x, $$-$$$), Player Tracking/GPS ("Every field based session," $$$),
Aerobic Tests via Heart Rate Recovery (1x, $-$$), Training Load (sRPE x Duration, "Best
athletes," ES, $), Monotony (Average Daily Training Load / Standard Deviation of Weekly
Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Strain (Monotony x Weekly Training Load, "Best
athletes," ES, $), Heart Rate Variability ("√ or Best Athletes," ED, $-$$$). ("ES" and "ED"
are used on the slide without a stated legend; Inference: likely "Every Session" and "Every
Day" respectively, given the monitoring-schedule table on the following page (p.22) uses "ED"
for HRV and "ES" for RPE and Bosco jump testing, both of which are typically administered
daily or every session.)

**Why it works** - The slides state which tools exist and at what frequency and (for
Psychological and Physical Fitness) cost, but do not explain why each specific frequency was
chosen (e.g., why skinfolds biweekly-or-monthly rather than weekly) beyond the general "start
simple and small, be very consistent" philosophy stated on the closing slide (see
[[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]]).

**When to apply** - As a menu for building a monitoring program within resource constraints,
by choosing tools across the four domains that fit a program's budget (using the cost tiers as
a guide where given) and testing capacity (using the frequency guidance and the "Best
Athletes"-only option for more expensive or time-consuming tools). Eric's baseline: it
documents a broadly consistent multi-domain approach at Baylor (force-plate CMJ testing,
GPS/Catapult load monitoring, SmartSpeed timing, VALD suite tools, `method-baseline.md`,
"Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," "Load monitoring and GPS," "Speed and sprint").
Inference: this Evans framework's cost-tiering and "Best Athletes only" triage concept is not
explicitly named in the baseline material reviewed, though Eric's baseline's decision to
retire roster-wide NordBord testing in favor of targeted use for "smaller numbers, clear
clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`) reflects the same underlying
triage logic this framework's "Best Athletes" column encodes for other tools. Inference: the
p.16 "Body Comp Analyzers... no more than 4x per year" figure matches, number for number, the
rule Eric's baseline records as "author uncertain" (`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body
composition," line 130, citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`); this slide may be the
origin of, or a shared source with, that baseline rule, though this is not confirmed.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The "ES" and "ED" abbreviations are not defined on the
slide itself; the reading given above is Inference from context (the monitoring-schedule table
on the following page), not a stated definition, and should be verified against the CVASPS
transcript or another source before being treated as certain. No cost tier is given for the
Nutrition/Body Composition or Movement/Muscle domains. The Monotony and Strain formulas are
given without a worked numeric example or citation to the original sports-science literature.
Inference (reviewer knowledge): the monotony and strain formulas match Foster's (1998) model,
but the slide does not name Foster or any other source. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No single-athlete worked example combining tools across all four domains is
given in this lecture; the monitoring-schedule table (p.22) shows a 12-week schedule template
with HRV (ED), RPE (ES), Bosco jump testing (2x), Bodyweight (1x), Body Fat % (occasional
checkmarks), and POMS/QUEST (occasional/ES) but does not name a specific athlete.

**Related** - [[framework--adime-monitoring-process]],
[[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]],
[[claim--big-data-monitoring-without-training-theory-is-noise]].
</content>

# "Monitoring Is a Compass, Not a GPS Unit"

**What it is** - Evans's closing slide (U4 L1 p.23, "closing thoughts") states, in words the
slide's own voice makes clearly his (this closing-thoughts section is written in first-person
coaching address throughout the lecture, unlike the unattributed textbook-style prose
elsewhere in this course): "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit. Only utilize it if you
believe in the literature and will utilize it to make adjustments to the training process.
Start simple and small, but be very consistent. Sometimes the cheaper options provide better
insight. Don't get offended if the data is showing your training plan is not working as well
as you think it should. LEARNING MOMENT!"

**Why it works** - This is a stated coaching philosophy about how to interpret monitoring
data, not a mechanism claim; Evans does not explain what makes monitoring "a compass" (general
directional guidance) rather than "a GPS unit" (precise positional data) beyond the framing
itself. Inference: the practical implication is that monitoring data should inform the
general direction of a training adjustment (are we trending toward fatigue, toward
readiness) rather than being trusted as a precise, standalone answer for exactly what to do
next - consistent with his own earlier conclusion that no single overtraining biomarker is a
definitive diagnostic (see [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]).

**When to apply** - As a framing reminder when introducing a monitoring program to staff or
athletes: expect directional trends, not precise answers, and be prepared to revise the
training plan when the data disagrees with it, treating that disagreement as useful
information rather than a threat. Eric's baseline: its own stated data-collection discipline
is "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the
insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Philosophy and decision principles," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), and its own
account of retiring subjective wellness surveys and roster-wide NordBord testing when they
stopped producing trustworthy, actionable signal (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and
GPS," "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: both share this heuristic's
premise that monitoring's value is instrumental (does it change what you do) rather than
automatic.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a general philosophy statement, not a specific
decision rule; it does not say which specific metrics function well as "compass"-type
directional signals versus which might mislead. "Start simple and small" and "sometimes the
cheaper options provide better insight" are stated as Evans's own recommendations without a
supporting citation or specific example of a cheap option outperforming an expensive one.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific worked example (a named metric or athlete case) is given on this
slide.

**Related** - [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]].
</content>

# Evans's Own Conclusion: No Definitive Diagnostic Tool for Overtraining Syndrome Exists

**What it is** - After surveying eight "hypothetical mechanisms" of overtraining syndrome
(OTS) across biochemistry, cardiovascular/HRV, immune system, hormonal, brain, training
status, psychometrics, and psychomotor speed (U3 L2 p.2-16), Evans's closing slide (p.17),
titled "Reality and OTS," states in his own words: "Definitive diagnostic tool for OTS is not
available. The human organisms of made of up many [sic] biological systems that are
independent and dependent upon each other, and the interaction between them is contextual on
the readiness and preparedness of those systems, the imposed stimuli, and the adaptation path
the individual makes to cope with the stressor. The reliance of adopting sound training theory
principles, and performance monitoring will continue to be paramount to keep athletes
improving in their respective sport." Along the way, he makes several specific claims: on
HRV, "HRV is a great way to assess persons ability to adapt to stressors" (p.9); on hormonal
markers, "hormonal markers are a potent tool to gauge disturbances" (p.12), and "Testosterone
/ Cortisol ratio used to be considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore"
(p.12); on immune markers, "there is NO evidence to low glutamine levels with impaired immune
function" (p.11); on the literature generally, "Research seems to be relatively scarce since
ensuring OTS is difficult... The biggest issue with the literature is the TIME at which they
are studying high level athletes" (p.10).

**Why it works** - This is Evans's own synthesized conclusion after reviewing multiple
candidate biomarker systems, not a mechanism claim. He calls HRV "a great way" (p.9) and
hormonal markers "a potent tool" (p.12), yet concludes no definitive tool exists (p.17); both
are recorded here rather than smoothed into a single verdict. Inference: the practical
implication is that overtraining should be inferred from the convergence of multiple
imperfect signals (training status, performance trend, and whichever biomarkers a program can
afford) rather than from any one test result in isolation. The U3 L1 p.19-26 Omegawave case
(see
[[claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]]) is
Evans's own applied example of exactly this kind of HRV-based monitoring, used alongside
training-load and readiness data rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic.

**When to apply** - As a caution against over-relying on any single monitoring metric (HRV,
cortisol, testosterone/cortisol ratio, glutamine) as a stand-alone overtraining diagnostic.
Eric's baseline: the department replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective
force-plate mRSI specifically because the surveys "couldn't be trusted" as a sole signal, and
mRSI itself is one part of a broader monitoring approach, not the sole diagnostic
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: this is directly consistent with Evans's
conclusion here. Eric's baseline: its tension #3 (coach's-eye-first versus objective-first) is
also relevant context. Inference: Evans's conclusion does not resolve that tension, since it
recommends "sound training theory principles, and performance monitoring" together, without
specifying how to weigh a coach's qualitative judgment against quantitative monitoring when
they disagree.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans's specific claims (HRV a "great way"; hormonal
markers a "potent tool"; testosterone/cortisol ratio no longer the "gold standard"; no
evidence linking low glutamine to impaired immune function) are stated without a named
citation in this lecture; treat them as his professional summary of a literature he does not
cite by author or year here, not as independently verified facts. Do not use this entry to
argue that monitoring is worthless; Evans's own conclusion explicitly retains "performance
monitoring" as "paramount," only rejecting the idea of a single definitive diagnostic test.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific athlete case is given on this slide; this is a literature-survey
conclusion. See [[claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness
-case]] (U3 L1 p.19-26) for Evans's applied HRV monitoring example from the preceding lecture.

**Related** - [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]] (U4 L1, Evans's later monitoring-process framework,
consistent with treating no-single-metric-is-sufficient as a design constraint),
[[claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]].
</content>

# Carl Valle's Critique, as Quoted by Evans: Monitoring Without Training-Theory Comprehension Is "Ornamental Data" and "a Suicide Mission"

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U4 L2 p.5) quotes Carl Valle directly: "Monitoring instead of
creating insight to the responses of athletes to training, is now creating a data and
information dark age in regards to the understanding of training, by poorly appreciating the
basic principles." And: "Without fully comprehending the training process, monitoring is
nothing more than observational recordings of a suicide mission, resulting in ornamental data
displayed real time for coaches to find a purpose because they are too fearful to train." No
publication or year is given for the quote beyond the name "Carl Valle." The surrounding
slides name a five-step "ACQUIRE, MANAGE, ANALYZE, VISUALIZE, ACTION" pipeline (p.6) and list
"Practical Reasons to Monitor" as Athlete Feedback, Coach Feedback, and Medical Team/Return to
Play (p.8); p.9-20 are equipment and product images (Catapult, timing gates, Omegawave,
BioForce, ithlete, Haloview dashboard, Firstbeat/Polar, Noraxon, Dartfish, and similar vendor
photos and video stills) with no argument text.

**Why it works** - This is a quoted critique from a named source (Carl Valle, previously
listed among Evans's "my influences" in U4 L1 p.2), not a claim Evans states in his own voice
in this slide; its argument, as quoted, is that monitoring technology can substitute for
(rather than support) genuine understanding of training theory, producing data that looks
authoritative ("ornamental data displayed real time") without actually informing coaching

information dark age in regards to the understanding of training, by poorly appreciating the
basic principles." And: "Without fully comprehending the training process, monitoring is

# Weight-Room Exercises Provide "Little Insight" on Field Performance When They Fail Dynamic-Correspondence Criteria

**What it is** - Evans states directly (U4 L1 p.5): "Most Important: Special Work Capacity...
Movement & Energetic potential relative to the sporting demands. Primary Questions (Needs
Analysis): What are the movements required? Dynamic Correspondence. What are the dominant
energy systems fueling those movements? Weight room exercises? Provide little insight on how
they will perform on their respective field of play. Why? Minimal DC criteria met." He then
immediately qualifies this, anticipating pushback (p.5): "Whoa there. You saying the weight
room is not important? Absolutely not!"

**Why it works** - Evans's own stated reasoning is that weight-room exercises typically meet
only some of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]] for the five-factor
checklist) relative to a given sport's actual competitive movements, so a weight-room test
result (e.g., a back squat max) does not directly indicate how that capacity will express
itself in the sport-specific movement pattern; he does not, in this slide, specify which of the
five Dynamic Correspondence criteria weight-room exercises typically fail, only that "minimal
DC criteria" are met in general.

**When to apply** - As a caution against treating weight-room testing (1RM lifts, jump tests
performed in isolation from the sport skill) as a direct proxy for on-field performance,
without denying that weight-room training itself contributes to Special Work Capacity. Eric's
baseline: "A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally...
even a valid test stops being valuable" without the infrastructure and interpretation context
to use it well (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`). Inference: Evans's claim here is a related but
distinct point: not about operational sustainability of a test, but about a testing method's
inherent limits in predicting a different outcome (field performance) than the one it
directly measures (weight-room capacity).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans does not name which specific weight-room exercises
he has in mind, nor does he give an example of measuring "how well" a given weight-room result
predicted (or failed to predict) actual field performance for any real athlete; this is a
conceptual claim, not a data-backed one, in this lecture. He also does not specify a threshold
for "minimal DC criteria met" versus a higher, more sport-corresponding threshold that would
change this conclusion. The course states a tension this entry must record rather than
smooth over: U3 L6 p.17 (Athletic Assessment, "Strength" slide) reports "1RM Squat Strength:
R=.76-.91 with various jumping and sprinting tasks; 1RM Bench Press: R=.88 and grinding
performance in elite sailors" - correlations between a weight-room 1RM test and jump/sprint
(and, for bench, sailing-grinding) performance, not on-field football performance. U2 L4 p.19
("Specificity") separately states that athletes "at a lower level of sports mastery may
benefit from nearly ANY TRAINING MODALITY and in turn could see positive transfer to commonly
executed sport tasks." Neither slide directly contradicts the "little insight" claim (the
R-values are correlations to jump and sprint tests, not to competitive on-field performance,
and the mastery qualifier is about training-modality transfer generally, not about weight-room
testing's predictive validity specifically), but both qualify it: the claim applies most
clearly to advanced athletes and to predicting on-field (not test-to-test) performance.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific exercise-to-sport-skill comparison is worked through in this
lecture; the wrestling takedown analysis from U2 L4 (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]]) is the course's only
detailed worked Dynamic Correspondence example, applied to a competitive skill rather than to
a weight-room exercise directly.

**Related** - [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]],
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]].
</content>

**What it is** - Evans states directly (U4 L1 p.5): "Most Important: Special Work Capacity...
Movement & Energetic potential relative to the sporting demands. Primary Questions (Needs
Analysis): What are the movements required? Dynamic Correspondence. What are the dominant
energy systems fueling those movements? Weight room exercises? Provide little insight on how
they will perform on their respective field of play. Why? Minimal DC criteria met." He then
immediately qualifies this, anticipating pushback (p.5): "Whoa there. You saying the weight
room is not important? Absolutely not!"

**Why it works** - Evans's own stated reasoning is that weight-room exercises typically meet
only some of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]] for the five-factor
checklist) relative to a given sport's actual competitive movements, so a weight-room test
result (e.g., a back squat max) does not directly indicate how that capacity will express
itself in the sport-specific movement pattern; he does not, in this slide, specify which of the
five Dynamic Correspondence criteria weight-room exercises typically fail, only that "minimal
DC criteria" are met in general.

performed in isolation from the sport skill) as a direct proxy for on-field performance,

connects directly to a broader theme in Eric's baseline: "A test can be scientifically valid

conceptual claim, not a data-backed one, in this lecture. He also does not specify a threshold

---
type: library-entry

domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: elite-sports-performance--evans
chapter: "U3 L1"
topic: sympathetic versus parasympathetic overtraining types, and an Omegawave HRV readiness case
category: [evans-citing, evans-framing, overtraining, monitoring, worked-example]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Overwork Splits Into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Forms, Illustrated by an Omegawave HRV Case

**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L1 p.15-18), following the four-stage Overtraining
Continuum (p.10, see [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]) and the blunted
double-exercise-challenge finding (p.11: cortisol, ACTH, PRL, and GH response curves for OTS
[dashed] versus NFO [solid] athletes across two exercise challenges separated by rest, with
ACTH, PRL, and GH showing a markedly blunted second-challenge response in OTS, captioned "OTS
have blunted responses in double exercise challenges"), split "Overwork" into two forms.
Monotonous overwork: "Results in a plateau or decline in performance as a result of
over-adaptation of the CNS to the use of non-varying motor patterns." Overwork generally:
"Can occur when an increased training volume or intensity is sustained for too long or
repeated too frequently. This overwhelms the athlete's ability to adapt." This branches into
Sympathetic Overwork ("Prolonged stress response," p.16) and Parasympathetic Overwork
("Advanced stage of overtraining in which the neuroendocrine system is compromised," p.16). A
comparison table (p.17, "SNS vs PSNS Overwork") assigns Sympathetic overtraining to "Team
sports, strength and power sports" (decreased motivation, increased irritability and
depression; decreased appetite; increased resting/exercise/recovery heart rate and blood
pressure, increased ECG abnormalities; increased cortisol, decreased testosterone, decreased
testosterone/cortisol ratio, increased catecholamine concentration, increased postexercise
hormonal recovery time; decreased muscle and liver glycogen, variable lactate response;
chronic fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance), and Parasympathetic overtraining to
"Endurance sports" (increased listlessness, depression, and sleeping; unchanged appetite;
increased resting bradycardia, decreased-or-unchanged exercise heart rate, increased-or-
unchanged postexercise heart-rate recovery, decreased-or-unchanged blood-pressure response;
decreased responsiveness to stressors; increased hypoglycemia during exercise, decreased
exercise and postexercise lactate; increased fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance). A
second, separately numbered table (p.18, "Table-1: Distinguishing Symptoms of Sympathetic and
Parasympathetic overtraining [2]," the bracketed "[2]" indicating the slide reproduces a
citation from an outside source Evans does not name on the slide) gives a longer symptom list
by the same two categories: fatigue (both), irritability vs. calmness, sleeplessness vs.
normal sleep, lack of appetite vs. normal appetite, weight loss vs. no change in weight, easy
sweating vs. normal sweating, nocturnal sweating (sympathetic only), frequent headaches vs. no
headaches, palpitation/chest pain (sympathetic only), rapid resting pulse vs. normal pulse,
increased basal metabolism vs. normal, slightly increased body temperature vs. normal, delayed
vs. normal pulse-rate recovery, faster breathing rate during exercise vs. no breathing
problems, decreased tolerance to stress (sympathetic only), poor coordination vs. clumsy
movements and poor coordination especially during hard exercise, shortened vs. normal reaction
time, shaky hands (sympathetic only), and restlessness/depressed mood vs. normal mood.

Immediately after (p.19-26), Evans presents six Omegawave HRV/readiness device screenshots for
what reads as a single unnamed athlete tracked over time (the screenshots are not individually
captioned with a name or date, so this continuity is Inference from the narrative sequence and
the p.24 "Comparing..." slide, not a stated fact). An early reading (p.19-20) shows: "Based on
the HRV assessment: Cardiac system is reasonably ready for any level of activity. Based on the
Omega assessment: CNS: High volume of Explosive and Explosive-Power activities are not
recommended." Readiness Indicators: Stress index 6 ("Within the norm"), Fatigue 7 ("Complete
recovery"), Adaptation reserves 6 ("High"); CNS 3 ("Reduced"); Metabolic reaction index 6,
value 400 (norm 100-500, "High"). The HRV detail slide (p.20) adds: "Stable adaptation to
stress. High functional reserve," bradycardia at 58 bpm, and parameters within norm (vagus
activity 0.28, norm 0.16-0.41; sympathetic activity 30, norm 15-55; tension index 54, norm
15-180). The spectrum breakdown (p.21) reads VLF 10.3%, LF 36.2%, HF 53.6%. A later reading
(p.22-23) shows decline: "Based on the HRV assessment: Active rest is preferred." Readiness
Indicators: Stress index 2 ("Distress"), Fatigue 1 ("Exhaustion"), Adaptation reserves 2
("Low"); Metabolic reaction index 5, value 269 ("Above average"). The HRV detail slide adds:
"Inadequate adaptation to stress. Low functional reserve. Excessive fatigue. Possible cardiac
system disturbance. Active rest preferred," tachycardia at 92 bpm, "Moderate sympathetic
hypertonia," and parameters outside norm (vagus activity 0.07, below the 0.16-0.41 norm;
tension index 582, far above the 15-180 norm). The p.24 "Comparing..." slide sets this reading
(VLF 16.6%, LF 43.0%, HF 40.4%) beside the earlier one. A further reading (p.25) is worse
still: "Unable to calculate spectrum due to significant rhythm disturbance." The final slide
(p.26) shows recovery, captioned "Blood work..." leading to "Less training / Improved
nutrition / Time," with the scattergram and histogram both tightening back toward the earlier,
healthier pattern.

**Why it works** — Neither the overwork-type tables nor the Omegawave case gives a mechanism
beyond what is quoted; the tables state associations (which sport type tends toward which
overtraining form, which symptoms go with which form) without explaining the underlying
physiology, and the Omegawave case is a set of vendor-software readouts, not an explained
causal account of why the athlete's readiness declined. Inference: read together, the
sequence argues that HRV/readiness monitoring (Omegawave here) can track an athlete moving
along the sympathetic-overtraining pattern described on p.17 (elevated tension index and
sympathetic activity, reduced HRV) and back out of it, which is consistent with why this case
immediately follows the sympathetic/parasympathetic tables in the lecture's structure, though
Evans does not state that connection explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** — As a two-category vocabulary for describing which direction an
overtrained athlete's presentation points (sympathetic: irritable, tachycardic, high cortisol,
common in team/power sports; parasympathetic: listless, bradycardic, low responsiveness to
stressors, common in endurance sports), and as a worked illustration of what a declining and
recovering HRV/readiness trend can look like on one commercial device. Eric's baseline: it
does not name sympathetic/parasympathetic overtraining or use Omegawave specifically; its own
monitoring stack centers on force-plate mRSI and the VALD suite rather than HRV
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: this framework
and case add HRV-specific vocabulary and a concrete device-output example not present in the
baseline material reviewed.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — The p.17 and p.18 tables carry no citation to a specific
paper on the slide itself (p.18's bracketed "[2]" shows the slide is reproducing someone
else's table, but the source is not named); do not treat the symptom lists as independently
verified without locating that source. The Omegawave case is a single unnamed athlete's
software output, not a validated case study with independent physiological confirmation, and
the entry writer's reading that all six screenshots belong to one athlete tracked over time is
Inference, not a stated fact on the slides. This entry also does not resolve, but records, a
tension elsewhere in the course: U3 L2 p.12 states the testosterone/cortisol ratio "used to be
considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]), while this lecture's p.17
table lists a decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio as one of several sympathetic-overtraining
signs; both are recorded rather than reconciled. Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The p.19-26 Omegawave readiness/HRV sequence, described in full above, is the
example: readiness index declining from "Complete recovery" (Fatigue 7, Stress index 6) to
"Distress / Exhaustion" (Fatigue 1, Stress index 2, tachycardia 92 bpm, tension index 582
against a 15-180 norm) to a reading where the spectrum could not be calculated "due to
significant rhythm disturbance," then recovering after "Blood work... Less training, Improved
nutrition, Time."

**Related** — [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (the four-stage continuum
this material follows in the same lecture),
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]] (U3 L2, the T/C-ratio
tension noted above, and Evans's later conclusion that HRV is "a great way to assess persons
ability to adapt to stressors" without being a stand-alone diagnostic).
</content>

14	# "Monitoring Is a Compass, Not a GPS Unit"
15	
16	**What it is** — Evans's closing slide (U4 L1 p.23, "closing thoughts") states (no attribution
17	shown): "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit. Only utilize it if you believe in the
18	literature and will utilize it to make adjustments to the training process. Start simple and
19	small, but be very consistent. Sometimes the cheaper options provide better insight. Don't get
20	offended if the data is showing your training plan is not working as well as you think it
21	should. LEARNING MOMENT!"
22	
23	**Why it works** — This is a stated coaching philosophy about how to interpret monitoring
24	data, not a mechanism claim; Evans does not explain what makes monitoring "a compass" (general
25	directional guidance) rather than "a GPS unit" (precise positional data) beyond the framing
26	itself. Inference: the practical implication is that monitoring data should inform the
27	general direction of a training adjustment (are we trending toward fatigue, toward
28	readiness) rather than being trusted as a precise, standalone answer for exactly what to do
29	next - consistent with his own earlier conclusion that no single overtraining biomarker is a
30	definitive diagnostic (see [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]).
31	
32	**When to apply** — As a framing reminder when introducing a monitoring program to staff or
33	athletes: expect directional trends, not precise answers, and be prepared to revise the
34	training plan when the data disagrees with it, treating that disagreement as useful
35	information rather than a threat. Eric's baseline: its own stated data-collection discipline
36	is "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the
37	insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting" (`method-baseline.md`,
38	"Philosophy and decision principles," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), and its own
39	account of retiring subjective wellness surveys and roster-wide NordBord testing when they
40	stopped producing trustworthy, actionable signal (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and
41	GPS," "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: both share this heuristic's
42	premise that monitoring's value is instrumental (does it change what you do) rather than
43	automatic.
44	
45	**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — This is a general philosophy statement, not a specific
46	decision rule; it does not say which specific metrics function well as "compass"-type
47	directional signals versus which might mislead. "Start simple and small" and "sometimes the
48	cheaper options provide better insight" are stated as Evans's own recommendations without a
49	supporting citation or specific example of a cheap option outperforming an expensive one.
50	Confidence is untested.
51	
52	**Example** — No specific worked example (a named metric or athlete case) is given on this
53	slide.
54	
55	**Related** — [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]],
56	[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]].

24	dissipate fatigue, induce adaptations, and increase the athlete's preparedness to perform at

48	constitutes adequate "recovery as a training means" for a given athlete or training phase.

52	given on this slide.

14	# Three Types of Overload: Stimulating, Retaining, Detraining
15	
16	**What it is** — Evans's slide (U2 L4 p.15) names "3 Types of Overload": (1) Stimulating -
17	"Magnitude of the training load is above the neutral level - heightened adaptation"; (2)
18	Retaining - "Magnitude is in the neutral zone - maintained preparedness"; (3) Detraining -
19	"Magnitude of the training load leads to a decrease in performance, the functional
20	capabilities of the athlete, or both." No author or citation is given for this specific
21	three-way naming on this slide, though it appears in the same lecture segment as other
22	Bondarchuk- and Issurin-cited material.
23	
24	**Why it works** — The slide defines each overload type by its outcome (heightened
25	adaptation, maintained preparedness, or decreased performance) relative to an unnamed
26	"neutral level," but does not state how to measure or identify that neutral level for a given
27	athlete; no mechanism is given for why loads above versus at versus below that level produce
28	these three different outcomes, beyond the general adaptation-stimulus logic given on the
29	preceding slide (U2 L4 p.14: "Increasing stimulus -> adaptation -> performance improvement...
30	Lack of stimulus -> plateau... Excessive stimulus -> maladaptation -> decrease in
31	performance").
32	
33	**When to apply** — As a three-way classification for describing the intent of a given
34	training block or phase: is this phase meant to stimulate new adaptation, retain current
35	fitness during a competing priority (e.g., in-season), or is it a planned detraining/deload
36	period. Eric's baseline: its in-season rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
37	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
38	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). Inference: this functions as a
39	Retaining-type overload strategy in this framework's terms, though the baseline material does
40	not use this specific three-way vocabulary.
41	
42	**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — The slide gives no numeric or percentage definition of the
43	"neutral level" that separates Stimulating from Retaining from Detraining loads for any
44	specific biomotor quality or athlete population; without that, this framework is a labeling
45	scheme for outcomes observed after the fact, not a prospective dosing tool. No citation is
46	given, so its origin (Bondarchuk, Issurin, or Evans's own synthesis of the surrounding cited
47	material) cannot be confirmed from this slide alone. Inference: a deliberate deload would only
48	fit "Detraining" if it lowers performance; the slide defines the type by that outcome, not by
49	whether the reduction was planned. Confidence is untested.
50	
51	**Example** — No worked example with specific loads or athletes is given in this lecture.
52	
53	**Related** — The "3 Basic Scenarios" slide (U2 L4 p.14) and the continuum slide (U2 L4 p.16,
54	a four-way "Undertraining / Overreaching / Overtraining" version plus Acute overload) share
55	this stimulus-to-outcome logic; see also
56	[[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (U3 L1) for Evans's later, more detailed
57	overtraining-specific version of this same underlying dose-response logic. Inference
58	(unverified reviewer suggestion, not yet checked against a primary source): the
59	stimulating/retaining/detraining terms with a "neutral zone" resemble Zatsiorsky and Kraemer,
60	*Science and Practice of Strength Training* (a listed HHPR 5355 textbook, `method-baseline.md`
61	line 219); if confirmed by a future reviewer, name it as the likely origin.

14	# Anokhin's Functional System: Central Nervous, Neuromuscular, and Energy-Supplying Subsystems Gathered Into One
15	
16	**What it is** — Evans's slide (U1 L3 p.10) credits "P. Anokhin" with a model in which the
17	"Human Organism" and "Its physiological systems" (Central nervous system, Neuromuscular
18	system, Energy-supplying system) are "Activated & Gathered into" a "FUNCTIONAL SYSTEM." The
19	next slide (p.12) states each subsystem's specific job in this functional system: the Central
20	nervous system's role is "Increasing capacity to produce the necessary intensity of impulses
21	from the central motor area to the periphery and to ensure appropriate intra and
22	inter-muscular coordination"; the Neuromuscular system's role is "Improving the function of
23	the motor apparatus in accordance with the work regime"; the Energy-supplying system's role
24	is "Enhancement of the energy providing sources and setting up the marriage between them."
25	The slide gives no citation year or source text for Anokhin's model.
26	
27	**Why it works** — The slide gives no mechanism for how these three subsystems are
28	"activated and gathered" into a single functional system beyond naming Anokhin as the
29	originator; it presents the three-part division and each part's stated role as given facts,
30	not as something derived from data shown on the slide. Inference: this framing appears
31	designed to argue that improving "power output" (the topic of the surrounding slides, see
32	[[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]]) requires improving all
33	three subsystems together, not any one in isolation, since the model calls them a single
34	integrated system rather than three independent parts.
35	
36	**When to apply** — As a three-part checklist (CNS, neuromuscular, energy-supply) when asking
37	whether a given training intervention is actually addressing the system that limits a
38	specific athlete's performance, rather than assuming any one subsystem (e.g., "more
39	strength") is always the answer. Eric's baseline: it does not name Anokhin or this specific
40	three-subsystem model; the closest baseline parallel is Eric's baseline: assessment is
41	continuous, not a single test day (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment").
42	
43	**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — The slide does not explain what would count as evidence
44	that a subsystem has been "improved," nor does it give any worked example applying this
45	three-part model to a specific athlete or sport within this lecture. The same subsystems
46	reappear as the rows of the U3 L7 p.3 athlete profile and in the U2 L4 p.27 "Performance
47	Chain" slide. Confidence is untested: this is a single unelaborated slide citing one named
48	author (Anokhin) with no year and no original text quoted.
49	
50	**Example** — Not given on the slide; Evans does not walk through a worked example of the
51	functional-system model in this lecture. Inference: U3 L7 p.3 (the ten-step annual-plan
52	profile table, see [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]) is the
53	course's closest applied use of the model.
54	
55	**Related** — [[framework--power-output-as-final-goal-of-competition-exercise]] (same
56	lecture, same "how do you improve power output" thread),
57	[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]].
58	</content>
