# Verkhoshansky's Activation Levels: Training, Quiet, High, Over-Activation, Stress, and the Threshold of Adaptability

**What it is** — Following the homeostasis/allostasis material earlier in the same lecture
(see [[framework--homeostasis-vs-allostasis-mcewen-sterling]]), Evans's slides (U1 L4
p.26-32), all credited "Verkhoshansky, 2012," present a training-load-response model. A
supercompensation diagram (p.26) shows repeated "Training work-out" -> "Body's hyperfunction"
-> "Repetitive work-recovery phases" (proteins depletion during work, re-synthesis during
recovery, each cycle net-positive) -> "Performance increasing," paired with a "Main aims of
training load flows" box mapping Strength, Speed, Aerobic Endurance, and Speed Endurance to
specific protein-synthesis targets (contractile protein; sarcoplasmic reticulum protein;
mitochondrial protein; proteins with buffer capacity and isoferment resistance to pH
decrease), then "Specific proteins depletion" -> "Increasing the specific proteins contents in
working organs thanks to the phenomenon of Supercompensation" -> "Specific
morphological-functional restructuring the athlete's body." A second chart (p.27) plots
Workability state, Metabolic processes activity, and Catabolic processes activity all rising
with training load, against a dotted Anabolic processes curve that rises then falls, overlaid
on five load bands: Training, Quiet Activation, High Activation, Over-Activation, Stress. A
third chart (p.28) adds "Critical level of homeostasis disturbance" and "Threshold of
adaptability" markers at the Over-Activation/Stress boundary, with the text: "When the
training load impact provokes the Over-Activation reaction, the prevalence of anabolic process
switches to catabolic. This change indicates the Threshold of adaptability has been surpassed,
which is also related to critical level of Homeostasis disturbance." Two further slides
("Ability for Athlete to Adapt," p.29-30) recast this as a balance-scale diagram (Constant
homeostasis disturbance versus Constant homeostasis re-establishing = Allostasis; the
imbalance = Allostatic load), with text: "Similarly, during execution of a training exercise,
surpassing the anaerobic threshold brings about glycolysis and the subsequent decrease in the
body's workability. During the training process, reaching beyond a certain level of training
load initiates stress syndrome and a consequent decrease in the body's adaptability" (p.29,
restated with near-identical wording on p.30, which also maps Low/Medium/High/Excessive load
onto Training/Activation/Stress states and Quiet/High/Over-Activation). Two final slides
(p.31-32) show "Subsequent loads impacts," each an arrow diagram of repeated training loads
against a "Critical level of homeostasis disturbance" line, with "Allostatic overload" marked
once the accumulated load supersedes that line: "Accumulation of allostatic load, which
supersedes the critical level of homeostatic disturbance, results in activation of the
emergency systems: allostatic overload" (p.31); "The human body cannot maintain such
allostatic load for very long without consequences. In the long run, allostatic changes may
fail to be adaptive as the maintenance of allostasis changes over a long period" (p.32). No
book title is given beyond "Verkhoshansky" and the year 2012.

**Why it works** — The slides state that crossing from Over-Activation into Stress marks a
shift from anabolic-dominant to catabolic-dominant processes (the "threshold of adaptability")
and that sustained allostatic load past that point produces "allostatic overload," but they do
not give a specific physiological mechanism for why this particular crossover happens where it
does, or how to measure "Over-Activation" versus "Stress" for a real athlete; the curves and
labels (Quiet/High/Over-Activation, Stress) are presented as a model, not derived from data
shown on the slide. Inference: read together with the earlier homeostasis/allostasis
definitions in the same lecture, this model's practical claim is that a single hard session can
be homeostatic (recoverable, p.26's supercompensation loop) while a sustained series of
sessions that keeps pushing past the threshold of adaptability becomes allostatic (the body
resets its operating level rather than simply recovering to the old one), but Evans does not
state this synthesis explicitly; it is the entry writer's reading across p.17-32 of this
lecture.

**When to apply** — As a vocabulary for describing where a training block sits on a
load-response spectrum: is a given session or block within the Training/Quiet/High-Activation
range (adaptive, anabolic-dominant, recoverable), at Over-Activation (the crossover point,
anabolic switching to catabolic), or past it into Stress/allostatic overload (unlikely to be
adaptive without a deliberate reduction in load)? Eric's baseline: it does not use this
specific activation-level vocabulary or "threshold of adaptability," though its own account of
retiring practices that stopped producing trustworthy signal, and its "recovery has to be
earned by training hard first" framing (`method-baseline.md`, "Recovery and sleep"),
operates on a related premise that training stress must stay within a productive range.
Inference: this framework gives that general premise a named, staged structure (five load
bands, a named crossover point) that the baseline material does not spell out.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — No book title, edition, or page number is given beyond
"Verkhoshansky, 2012," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this
ingest; a dedup grep of both the staging library and the vault for "threshold of adaptability,"
"over-activation," and "activation reaction" found no existing entry, so the homeostasis entry
in this same folder's earlier statement that this material "closely resembles already-staged
Supertraining content" is corrected here: no staged Supertraining entry currently contains this
specific model, so it is recorded as a new, not-yet-cross-checked entry rather than assumed to
duplicate one. The slides give no numeric thresholds (e.g., what training load, in any units,
constitutes "Over-Activation" for a given athlete); "Low/Medium/High/Excessive" and
"Training/Quiet/High/Over-Activation/Stress" are unitless, relative labels only. Confidence is
untested.

**Example** — No athlete-specific worked example is given; the model is presented generically
across all six slides described above.

**Related** — [[framework--homeostasis-vs-allostasis-mcewen-sterling]] (the immediately
preceding slides in the same lecture, defining homeostasis, allostasis, allostatic state, and
allostatic overload, which this framework applies directly to training load). Reciprocal-link
suggestion: `supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md`
and `supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus.md` cover related
Verkhoshansky training-load-to-adaptation material from the primary source; a reviewer with
both books staged should check whether this 2012-cited version adds or conflicts with either
entry, and whether Supertraining uses "threshold of adaptability" or "over-activation"
anywhere the grep above missed.
</content>

# Evans's Own "Notable Giants" Lineage of Sport Science and Coaching

**What it is** — On a single slide titled "Notable Giants" (U1 L2 p.3), Evans lists fourteen
lines naming fifteen named people alongside a one- or two-word role tag, with no further
elaboration on the slide itself: Nicholai Bernstein (Motor Control), L.P. Matveyev (Sport
Scientist / Coach), Yuri Verkhoshansky (Sport Scientist / Coach, starred), Carmelo Bosco
(Sport Scientist), Anatoliy Bondarchuk (Coach), Henk Kraaijenhof (Coach), Atko Viru and Mehis
Viru (Sport Scientist / Coach, starred, sharing one line), Charlie Francis (Coach, starred),
Michael Yessis (Professor / Coach, starred), Tudor Bompa (Coach / Professor), Vladimir Issurin
(Sport Scientist / Coach), Al Vermeil (Coach), Johnny Parker (Coach), and Dan Pfaff (Coach).
The slide does not explain what the asterisks mean; a plausible reading is "authors Evans has
read directly," but the slide gives no legend, so this is Inference, not a stated fact. A
separate slide in the same lecture (U1 L2 p.5) names a "Sport Coach: Randy Huntington" under a
low-resolution video still, disconnected from the named-giants list, with no other text.

**Why it works** — The slide gives no mechanism or rationale for why this list, in this
order, constitutes "the" lineage; it functions as a syllabus of names to know rather than an
argued history. Inference: the list moves roughly from foundational Soviet motor-control and
periodization theory (Bernstein, Matveyev) through Soviet/Eastern-bloc training-methods
figures (Verkhoshansky, Bosco, Bondarchuk, the Virus) to Western popularizers and coaches
who studied or translated that material (Kraaijenhof, Francis, Yessis, Bompa, Issurin,
Vermeil, Parker, Pfaff), but this grouping logic is not stated on the slide itself.

**When to apply** — Useful as a checklist for which authors' names a student of this course
is expected to recognize before later lectures cite them. Issurin (2008) and Bompa (2009) are
cited by name and year in U3 L4-L5; Verkhoshansky and Bondarchuk reappear by name only in the
U3 L4 p.2 acknowledgements (which also add William Freeman, Vern Gambetta and Peter Tschiene);
see [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]. (The former
[[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]] entry this line used to cross-link
was deleted as a duplicate of primary-source Issurin content; see
`block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md` and
`block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules.md`.)
Eric's baseline: it names an overlapping but not identical set as course-team influences
(Vermeil, Bondarchuk, Verkhoshansky, Zatsiorsky, Parker/Miller/Panariello, Prilepin, Fober;
`method-baseline.md`, "Named influences" table). Inference: this suggests convergence between
the HHPR 5355 course material and Evans's own course on which names matter, though the two
lists are not identical (Evans names Bernstein, Bosco, the Virus, Kraaijenhof, Yessis, and
Issurin, none of which appear in Eric's baseline's named-influences table; Pfaff appears in
both; Eric's baseline names Zatsiorsky, Panariello, Prilepin, and Fober, none of which appear
on this Evans slide).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** — This is a bare name list with role tags, not a
substantive claim about any individual's ideas; treat it only as an index of who to expect
Evans to cite later, not as evidence for any specific training method. The slide gives no
sourcing for why these fifteen names and not others, so completeness cannot be assessed.
Confidence is untested: this is one slide from a practitioner course, uncorroborated by any
other source in this library.

**Example** — When Evans later cites "Bondarchuk" for a 3-principle training-system model
(U2 L4, see [[framework--bondarchuk-three-principles-of-training-system-construction]]) or
"Bompa, 2009" for annual-plan structure (U3 L4-L5), this slide is the place those names were
first introduced in the course, unglossed.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-three-principles-of-training-system-construction]],
[[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion:
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/_book.md` and `transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/_book.md`
could each note that this course-lecture entry independently lists their authors among a
lineage of "giants," as a light corroboration of those authors' standing in the field
(not of any specific claim).
</content>
